verified.title: The Progressed Horoscope ('Astrology for All' Series Vol. V), Part III, Chapter XVII 'Solar Revolutions or Birthday Maps', Example I
verified.page: pp. 236-237 (method, natal Sun, Example I computation) and p. 240 (result); chart p. 234; birth data p. 26. Scan leaves n199, n200, n203, n197, n40
verified.subject: Queen Mary (Mary of Teck), consort of George V
verified.explanation:
The engine reproduces the source to about 1 s.

- **Where the -1.03 s comes from:** it is entirely the natal-longitude difference. The engine's natal Sun for 1867-05-26 23:59 UT is Gemini 5°12'24.96". The source's radical Sun is Gemini 5°12'25" (printed on p. 237 and in the p. 28 natal chart). That is -0.04", and the Sun moves about 0.04" per second of time.
- **With the source's own radical longitude:** solarReturnInstant gives 1910-05-27T09:39:03.997Z, which is -0.003 s from the stated time.
- **Noon positions:** the engine's apparent Sun at 12:00 UT is Gemini 4°20'28.87" on 26 May and 5°18'03.01" on 27 May 1910. The source's figures imply 4°20'29" (radical minus 51'56") and 5°18'03" (plus 57'34"). So the source's ephemeris agrees with the engine to about 0.1". It uses apparent longitudes of date, since a missing aberration or nutation would show up as tens of arcseconds.
- **The source's own arithmetic:** its five-figure ternary proportional logs give 21h 39m 4s, while the exact proportion 24h x 3116/3454 of its figures gives 21h 39m 5.1s. That is about 1 s of rounding.
- **Precision of the inputs:** the source's longitudes are rounded to 1" of arc, which is worth up to about 25 s of time. The near-zero difference is therefore partly coincidence inside the source's rounding.
- **Tables named:** Chambers's Mathematical Tables for the TP logs (footnote, pp. 236-237). The 1910 ephemeris is unnamed ("an ephemeris for that year").
issues: Printing error, checked on the p. 236 page image (scan file _0199), not an OCR fault: it prints 'differences of 9h 30m and 13h 51m'. The stated times give 9h 40m (11.59 p.m. to 9.39 a.m.) and 12h 51m (Besant, 5.29 p.m. to 6.20 a.m.). Recorded, not corrected. It does not affect the return instant.

p. 237 (scan file _0200) prints the TP log (arithmetical complement) of 57'34" as '9 50480'. The printed column sum '91979' needs 9.50490, which is the correct value, so the addend is a typo. The result is unaffected.
The source's TP-log working gives 21h 39m 4s. The exact proportion of its own figures (57'34" : 51'56" :: 24h) gives 21h 39m 5.1s, about 1 s of arithmetic rounding in the source.
The fraction printed after '21 39' in the TP-log column (probably 2/33) cannot be read reliably in the low-resolution scan. The text says it is 'equivalent to 4 seconds, to the nearest second'.

The italic heading of the p. 28 natal chart reads ambiguously as '11 59' or '11 50' p.m. in the scan. The text on pp. 26, 27, 37 and 236 says 11.59 p.m. The radical Sun 5°12'25" fits 23:59 GMT (engine 5°12'24.96"); 23:50 would give about 5°12'03".
The 1910 ephemeris is not named; the text says only 'an ephemeris for that year'. The tables named are Chambers's Mathematical Tables, for the TP logs.

Not verified by me, and not needed for the fixture: the candidate's provenance claims about the second-edition copy (modern-astrology-alan-leo_202605) and Randall's 1917 index. What I verified is the 5th edition: the publisher's announcement (scan file _0001) lists editions 1906, 1913, 1923, 1929, 1936.

Return chart p. 234 (scan file _0197): I checked Sun 5.12.25, Mercury 2.38 R and Saturn 1.10 against the image. The MC 0.44 reading comes only from a low-resolution full-page view, and I did not check the other chart positions the candidate lists. They are not needed for the return instant.

The candidate quote is a composite with ellipses. Its first half is p. 237 ('The Sun's place at birth is shown in the horoscope in Chapter VI to have been [Gemini] 5° 12' 25"') and its second half p. 240 ('equivalent to 9h 39m 4s a m, G M T, on 27th May'). Subject's death is not in the source (a 1936 printing). Wikipedia 'Mary of Teck' (fetched 2026-11-01) gives death 24 March 1953 at Marlborough House, and birth 26 May 1867 at Kensington Palace, which matches the source's nativity.

verified.title: The Progressed Horoscope ('Astrology for All' Series Vol. V), Part III, Chapter XVII 'Solar Revolutions or Birthday Maps', Example III
verified.page: p. 237 (natal Sun to seconds), p. 236 (summary), p. 238 (chart), p. 241 (Example III); birth data p. 281 (Ch. XXI). Scan leaves n200, n199, n201, n204, n242
verified.subject: Mrs Annie Besant
verified.explanation:
The engine's return is 3.04 s later than the stated one, which is well inside the source's own rounding.

(1) Natal Sun. The engine puts it at ♎7°54'06.79" (187.9018875°), against Leo's ♎7°54'07" on p. 237, a difference of -0.21". Leo's inputs agree with the engine. His noon place of ♎7°40'37" is 0.04" from the engine's value at 1847-10-01 12:00 UT. His daily motion of 59'5" is 0.1" from the engine's 59'5.11". Redoing his p. 237 proportion with the engine's places rounded to whole seconds gives exactly 7°40'37", 59'5" and 7°54'7". So the 0.21" comes from linear proportion over 5h29m plus rounding. It makes the engine's return 5.0 s earlier.

(2) Return to that longitude. The engine's Sun reaches Leo's 7°54'7" at 06:20:20.04 UT, 8.0 s after his time; at his time it stands at 7°54'06.67". Leo's 1907 working is not printed. Applying his Example I method (linear proportion between Greenwich noons) to the engine's 1907 noon places, rounded to whole seconds (♎7°09'00" and ♎8°08'03"), gives 06:20:13.2 GMT. That is 1.2 s from his figure. The 8 s splits roughly as:
- about 5 s from linear interpolation while the Sun is speeding up in October;
- about 2 s from rounding the noon places;
- about 1 s from the TP-log arithmetic and the final rounding.

(3) ΔT. The engine applies about 8.6 s in 1847 and 8.4 s in 1907; the almanacs Leo copied did not. This shifts the Sun by about 0.35" in the same direction at both dates, so it largely cancels in a return.

The planets in Leo's return chart also match the engine at 06:20:12 UT:
- within 1' for the Sun, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune;
- 0.8' for the Moon and 1.5' for Mercury.

No error in the source affects the return instant.
issues: The p. 236 summary sentence misprints the two intervals as 'differences of 9h 30m and 13h 51m', and the page image confirms this is how it is printed. The true intervals are 9h 40m (11.59 p.m. to 9.39 a.m.) and 12h 51m (5.29 p.m. to 6.20 a.m.). The return instant itself is consistent on p. 236 (6.20 a.m.), p. 238 and p. 241 (6h 20m 12s).

The archive.org djvu.txt OCR garbles key figures. It reads 'Add o 13 10' where the page prints 0 13 30, '20® 12* a m' where the caption prints 6h 20m 12s, 'and October at 620 am', and 'i3h'. All numbers were read from the page images: leaves n199 (p. 236), n200 (p. 237), n201 (p. 238), n204 (p. 241) and n242 (p. 281).

The birth time is Leo's rectified 5.29 p.m.: p. 281 says it was rectified by primary arcs, and her autobiography gives 5.39 p.m. Using 5.39 p.m. would move the return by about +10 min, so the fixture must use 5.29 p.m. and record that it is a rectified time.

The fixture must enter the birth as GMT 17:29:00, as Leo does on p. 237. Reading it as London LMT (0°05'-0°08' W) would make the engine's return 23-33 s later than the stated time, still within 40 s but on a different basis.

The return chart's angles only show that Leo applied no London longitude correction. They cannot tell GMT at 0° from London LMT at 0°05' W, because both give the same local sidereal time. The GMT basis of the instant rests on the p. 237 method and on the G.M.T. labels of Examples I and II (pp. 240-241).
Leo's 1907 working for Example III (noon places and proportion) is not printed, only the result. The 5 s / 2 s / 1 s breakdown is my reconstruction using the method of Example I.

Provenance: the copy read is the 5th edition of 1936 (title page: Modern Astrology Office, also L. N. Fowler, 1936; edition list 1906, 1913, 1923, 1929, 1936). It was printed after Leo's death (Wikipedia: 30 Aug 1917). The example is absent from the 1906 first edition: the archive.org full text bub_gb_OY7ZLx4jQmcC has no Besant or 1907 example. I could not check the candidate's claims about the 1913 2nd edition, Randall's 1917 index, or a copy with a 'Note to the Second Edition'. The index is not openly online, and the 1969 archive.org copy is lending-only. Cite the 1936 printing, pp. 236-238, 241 and 281.

Annie Besant's death is confirmed by Wikipedia ('Annie Besant': '1 October 1847 - 20 September 1933', died at Adyar) and by theosophy.wiki ('Annie Besant died at Adyar, Madras, on September 20, 1933'). Britannica returned HTTP 403.

verified.explanation:
Engine natal Sun: 72.4316969° = Gemini 12°25'54.11". Source radical Sun: Gemini 12°25'54" (p. 55 text and p. 40 chart). The two differ by 0.11". The engine's return is 1893-06-02T19:54:12.905Z from both solarReturnInstant and solarReturn, with no flags. That is 12.9 s after the stated 19:54:00, or 12.4 s after the source's unrounded 19:54:00.5. The engine's return to the source's own 12°25'54" is 19:54:10.2, so 2.7 s of the difference comes from the 0.11" natal difference (1" ≈ 25.08 s at 57'25"/day).

The other ~10 s comes from the 1893 ephemeris figures, which the source rounds to whole arcseconds. Its working implies a Greenwich-noon Sun of Gemini 12°07'00" (12°25'54" − 18'54") and a daily motion of 57'25". The engine has 12°06'59.5" and 57'25.2". Half an arcsecond at the noon place is about 12.5 s of time.

Differences between the period tables' time argument and UT1 are at most ~8 s of the Sun's motion. The engine's ΔT is +7.9 s in 1865 and −4.8 s in 1893, which moves the Sun by under 0.33".

The chain is consistent throughout. At the stated 19:54:00 GMT the engine's angles are Asc Sagittarius 10°46.8' and MC Libra 10°43.0', against the printed ♐10.47 and ♎10.43. The engine's return planets match the p. 54 chart within about 1': Sun 12°26', Venus 20°51', Neptune 11°03.5', Mars Cancer 12°38', Saturn Libra 6°02' R, Uranus Scorpio 7°21' R. The exception is Mercury, 9°29.6' against 9°31'.

So the difference is fully explained by the source's whole-arcsecond positions and its rounding to the minute.

Re-read from the Google Books page images (id ySASAAAAYAAJ). The title page reads 1903, L. N. Fowler & Co., 7 Imperial Arcade, or "Modern Astrology" Office, 9 Lyncroft Gardens. Chapter III's title is on p. 21. On p. 24 the anchor reads "reach this longitude on 9th November, 1900, at 6h. 10m. 27s. p.m.", with the radical Sun 16°54'20" Scorpio and 59 years × 50.2572" = 49'25", giving the variant 17°43'45" on 10 Nov 1900 at 1h. 50m. 9s. p.m. The p. 23 map shows that variant (London). The discussion is on p. 25.

Full chain: the engine's natal Sun for 10:48:34 UT is 16°54'21.90" Sco, 1.90" more than Green's 16°54'20". Its return is 18:11:33.241Z, +66.2 s from the stated time. Other birth readings give +32.2 s (10:48:00 UT, natal 16°54'20.47") and +72.2 s (10:48:40 UT, natal 16°54'22.15").

Return step alone: using Green's own radical longitude as input, the engine gives 18:10:47.954Z, +21.0 s. The engine Sun at 18:10:27 UT is 16°54'19.12", 0.88" short. Green's own two crossings are 49'25" apart in 70,782 s, i.e. 23.87 s of time per arcsecond, so this is under 1".

Cross-check against JPL Horizons DE441 (quantity 31, apparent ecliptic of date, UT):
- The engine is +6.2 s on the chain and -10.6 s on the return step.
- Green's crossing for his own longitude is 31.5 s earlier than DE441 (DE441: 18:10:58.5).
- His variant crossing is 26.3 s earlier than DE441 (DE441: 13:50:35.3; engine minus Green there = +16.1 s).
- DE441 itself would be +60.0 s from Green on the same chain.

So the gap comes mainly from the source, not the engine:
(1) Green's radical is 1.2" below DE441 for 10:48 local mean time, although it is within 0.2" of DE441 for 10:48 Greenwich time. This is worth about 28 s.
(2) Both of his 1900 crossings run 26-32 s early against DE441. Either his unnamed 1900 tables put the Sun about 1.1-1.3" ahead, or his "London" times are London local mean time, in which case he matches DE441 to a few seconds. The source does not say which.
(3) The engine's own error here is about 6-11 s.

Both are inside the half-minute rounding the author states on p. 56, where the maps are "calculated to the nearest minute (of time) only". The difference is rounding, not an error in the source.

The engine supports this reading in three ways:
- **Planets:** at 01:59 GMT the engine reproduces every body on Map No. 1 within about 1′:
  - Sun 11°♑0.8′ (printed 11°1′)
  - Mars 11°♍47.5′ (printed 11°47′)
  - Saturn 7°♑49.7′ (printed 7°50′)
  - Venus 12°♐5.8′ (printed 12°6′)

  - Jupiter 26°♐12.1′ (printed 26°13′)
  - Uranus 14°♐22.2′ (printed 14°23′)
  - Mercury 29°♐19.9′ (printed 29°♐21′, below the map)
- **Cusps:** Placidus cusps at Kensington round to the printed whole-degree cusps:
  - Asc 28°♎31′ to ♎29°, which matches the text's "extreme end of Libra is rising"
  - MC 8°♌09′ to ♌8°
  - 2nd 25°♏38′ to ♏26°
  - 3rd 29°♐36′ to ♑0°

  - 12th 8°♎27′ to ♎8°

The natal chain cannot be tested from this source because the article states no birth instant. It takes the radical Moon from E. H. Bailey's horoscope (Vol. X, p. 112). - Jupiter is at 27°46′ Scorpio, near the MC at 25°49′ Scorpio.
- Mercury (5°52′ Sagittarius, retrograde) and Uranus (9°11′ Sagittarius) are close by.

Engine minus stated is +387.157 s for the whole chain. The natal longitude accounts for +389.4 s of it. The source's radical Sun is Aries 29°44′55.0″ (p. 121; Fig. 5 shows 29°44′55″). At the source's own birth instant, the engine's apparent Sun is Aries 29°45′10.82″, 15.82″ higher. At the Sun's April 1870 rate of 2.4378″ per minute, 15.82″ is 389.4 s.

The birth instant is not the cause. The source's natal RAMC matches the engine to 0.5 s at 1h Paris mean time. JPL Horizons (quantity 31, UT1) gives 29.7527010°, which is 29°45′09.72″, also 14.7″ above the source. So the error is in the source's 1808 Sun, and the source does not say how it computed that value.

The size of the error matches the nutation in longitude at the birth: the engine gives +13.1″ then. A radical longitude referred to the mean equinox would explain most of the gap, but this is not proven.

Starting from the source's own radical longitude, solarReturnInstant gives 1870-04-20T01:21:37.757Z, 2.243 s before the stated time. The source's method accounts for all of it:
- −1.01 s from rounding. Exact proportion of its printed inputs gives 13h 21m 38.99s; the book prints 13h 21m 40s.
- +3.80 s because the engine's Greenwich-noon longitudes are 0.183″ and 0.132″ below the source's Nautical Almanac values, 29°12′20.7″ and 30°10′51.2″. Horizons is 0.38″ and 0.32″ below them.
- −5.04 s because simple proportion over 24 h ignores the Sun's second difference of −1.67″ per day.
issues: Whole-chain failure: the source's radical Sun, 29°44′55.0″, is about 15″ below the Sun at the source's own birth instant: −15.82″ against the engine and −14.72″ against JPL Horizons. That instant is confirmed by the source's natal RAMC to 0.5 s. This moves the return by about 6.5 min. The source states its radical longitude to 0.1″ and gives no basis for its 1808 Sun, so no source-justified tolerance covers +387 s.

A direct fixture would be usable: solarReturnInstant(29°44′55.0″ = 29.7486111°, near 1870-04-20) against 1870-04-20T01:21:40 UT1. The engine gives 01:21:37.757, a difference of −2.24 s, with every part accounted for. This tests the solver and the 1870 Sun, not the natal-chart step.

The time basis of the birth is not stated on p. 100. Paris local mean time is inferred from the source's RAMC (p. 101). If the 1h were apparent solar time, the birth would move by the equation of time, about 1 min in late April, but the source's RAMC shows it used mean time.
The engine's 1808 natal Sun is +1.10″ from Horizons (29.7530060° against 29.7527010°). That is within the engine's documented accuracy and is worth about 27 s of the chain difference.

verified.explanation:
Engine minus stated is +799.6 s with the birth read as London apparent time. Read as GMT it is +993.2 s; as London LMT, +1016.4 s.

**Natal Sun (+904.3 s).** Almost all of the difference is the natal Sun's arc-seconds that the source drops. It states the radical Sun as '2° 6′ of Gemini' and solves for exactly 2°6′00″. The engine's Sun at the stated birth is ♊2°6′36.19″ (♊2°6′43.94″ if read as GMT), so the source evidently truncated. 36.19″ at the engine's 144.07″/h is +904.3 s (43.94″ gives +1098.0 s).

**Author's tables (−88.9 s).** His 1854 noon places are 3.52″ and 3.39″ behind the engine at Greenwich mean noon. So the engine's Sun reaches 2°6′00″ at 15:03:10.3 UT, 88.9 s before the exact proportion of his printed places (15:04:39.2).

**Author's rounding (−15.8 s).** He took the arc still to go, 7′23.4″ (the exact difference of his printed values), as 7′24″, and rounded 3h 4m 54.2s up to 55s.

Check: 904.3 − 88.9 − 15.8 = 799.6 s. Given the source's own radical (62.1°) directly, the engine is only 104.7 s before the stated clock time.

**Error in the source.** The proportion's answer, '3h. 51m. 55s. P. M.' (printed twice), is a misprint. The printed proportion 7′24″ : 57′37.8″ :: x : 24h gives 3h 4m 54.2s. The figure's planets fit about 15:05 GMT, not 15:52: the engine Moon is ♈25°22′19″ at 15:04:55 against ♈25°47′ at 15:51:55, and the figure prints ☽ 25°22′. Mercury ♉25°29′, Mars ♍7°45′, Saturn ♊4°48′ and Jupiter ♑27°26′R also agree with the engine to within 1′ at 15:04:55.
issues: Three different return times are printed. '3h. 51m. 55s. P. M.' is the proportion answer (twice, p. 11); '3h. 4m. 55s.' is the 'Clock time' (p. 11) and the figure heading; '3h. 4m. 35s.' is in para 9 (p. 11). Only 3h 4m 55s follows from the printed proportion (444″/3457.8″ × 24h = 3h 4m 54.2s), and it alone matches the printed RAMC and the figure's Moon. The fixture must use the clock time and record the others. Measured against 3h 51m 55s, the engine would be −2020 s off.

The printed noon value '4° 3′ 55″' is labelled 'Sol's Right Ascension' and uses degree marks for h m s. With the printed '0 0 32' it does not add to the printed RAMC 7h 8m 32s. 4h 3m 5s + 3h 4m 55s + 32 s does, and GMST at 12:00 UT on 23 May 1854 is 4h 3m 6.6s, so '55″' looks like a misprint for 5″. The acceleration for 3h 5m should also be about 30 s, not 32 s. Recorded as printed, not corrected.

The natal time basis is not stated. The source's own natal figure (RAMC 301°8′, Asc ♊1°14′, ☽ ♊3°33′) fits the time read as London apparent time: engine RAMC 301°9.8′, Asc ♊1°13′47″, ☽ ♊3°34.3′. The radical Sun is given only to the arc-minute ('2° 6′'), and the return is solved for exactly 2°6′00″. The engine's natal Sun is 2°6′36.19″ (apparent reading) or 2°6′43.94″ (GMT), so the source evidently truncated. That loss alone is 15 to 18 minutes of solar motion.
The ephemeris is not named. Its 1854 noon Sun places sit 3.4 to 3.5″ behind the engine (88.9 s of time); they fit Greenwich mean noon.
The author rounded the arc still to go, 7′23.4″, to 7′24″, which adds +15 s.

verified.explanation:
The engine's full chain lands 261.15 s (4m 21s) after Pearce's stated return. Almost all of the gap comes from Pearce's tables, not the engine.

(1) Natal Sun, +349.6 s. Pearce's radical is ♊2°6′57″. At UT 04:15:51 the engine gives ♊2°7′10.99″ (62.1197205°), 13.99″ more. JPL Horizons (apparent ecliptic of date, UT1) gives ♊2°7′10.87″, so the engine is confirmed to 0.12″. At 24.985 s per arcsecond near 23 May 1854, 13.99″ is +349.6 s.
The cause is in his printed inputs on p. 70, taken 'from either the Nautical Almanac or White's Ephemeris for 1819'. His noon Suns are ♊1°27′53″ (May 23) and ♊2°25′32″ (May 24). Horizons at Greenwich mean noon gives ♊1°28′7.47″ and ♊2°25′45.29″, so his values are 14.47″ and 13.29″ low.
The Nautical Almanac tabulated for Greenwich apparent time through its 1833 issue (Wikipedia, 'The Nautical Almanac'). The Sun crossed the Greenwich meridian at 11:56:20 and 11:56:25 UT on those days. Measured at those apparent noons, his values are only 5.8″ and 4.8″ low. So the apparent-noon basis plus about 5″ of table error probably explains it, but I did not read the 1819 almanac to check.
His sidereal time at noon, 4h 1m 1.2s, is a mean-noon value: the IAU 1982 GMST at mean noon is 4h 1m 2.9s.
Two small slips cancel. His printed proportion 39′4″ should be 57′39″×16¼/24 = 39′2.03″, which makes his radical 1.97″ high. He also interpolated 16¼ h from Greenwich noon without the 51 s of west longitude that his RAMC uses, which costs 2.04″ the other way.

(2) 1854 ephemeris, −88.5 s. At his stated instant the engine Sun is ♊2°7′0.54″ (Horizons ♊2°6′59.88″), which is 3.5″ (Horizons 2.9″) past his radical. So the engine's solarReturnInstant for ♊2°6′57″ falls at 15:26:54.507 UT, 88.5 s early. His 1854 values or proportion, which are not printed, ran about 3″ low. On p. 120 he names 'the Nautical Almanac or Zadkiel's Ephemeris' for returns.

verified.explanation:
The full engine chain uses the engine's own natal Sun, Sag 17deg40'16.6" at 13:00 LMT (the source says 17deg40'11"), then solarReturn. It puts the 1823 return at 11:27:58 UT, which is 11:27:27.5 London mean time. Zadkiel's "11h. 30m. A.M." has no stated time basis, and the engine falls between its two readings:
- Read as mean (clock) time, like his natal time, the engine is 152.5 s earlier.
- Read as apparent time (11:22:50.5 mean), the engine is 277 s later.

What favours each reading:
(1) The instant is not worked on the page, and the author says a revolution "may readily be estimated to within a trifle". 11h 30m is exactly the birth time (1 P.M. mean) plus 8 mean tropical years: 11:30:02 to 11:30:32 for years of 365.24219 to 365.24223 days. So it is most likely a mean-motion estimate in mean time. The true apparent Sun does not move at the uniform mean-year rate. The nutation in longitude went from -17.7" to +15.6" between the two dates, about 13 min of solar motion, partly offset by orbital and perturbation terms. Together these account for the engine's -2.5 min.
(2) The printed revolution places were taken 23h 30m after White's apparent noon of 9 Dec, without an equation-of-time correction. The printed Moon, Pis 14deg12' with declination 2deg15', matches the engine's Moon at 11:30 apparent (Pis 14deg12.4', S2deg15'). At 11:30 mean the engine has Pis 14deg16.1'. His natal Moon, Ari 5deg39', agrees with the engine to 0.6', so a 3.9' gap would be out of character. The apparent reading therefore cannot be excluded.
(3) The ephemeris: White's apparent-noon Sun for 10 Dec 1815, Sag 17deg37'21", is 3.6" below the engine's 17deg37'24.6". That is why Zadkiel's natal Sun is 5.6" below the engine's. Using Zadkiel's own natal 17deg40'11", the engine returns at 11:25:45 UT: -285.6 s on the mean reading, +143.9 s on the apparent reading. For an ephemeris-derived 11:30 apparent, White's 1823 Sun would have to be about 7" ahead of the engine, because the engine reaches 17deg40'11" at about 11:33 apparent.

Nothing in this requires an error in the source.

A.M." is either London mean time (1823-12-10T11:30:30.6Z, engine -152.5 s) or apparent time (11:23:21.1Z, engine +277.0 s); the two are 429.5 s apart. verified.explanation:
The engine is 277.6 s later than the stated time, read as apparent time. The difference has two parts:

(1) The natal Sun accounts for +125.7 s. The engine's natal Sun is ♐17°40′16.3″, which is 5.3″ past the source's 17°40′11″ (p. 34). The engine's return to the source's own 17°40′11″ is 11:25:45.0Z. The source's value comes from White's Ephemeris, whose noon Sun is ♐17°37′21″. That is 4.6″ below the engine's apparent Sun at the same London apparent noon (17°37′25.6″ at 1815-12-10T11:53:13.5Z). On top of that, Zadkiel rounds slightly: he takes the proportional part for 1h 7m instead of 1h 7m 8s, and a daily motion of 61′.

(2) The 1823 side accounts for +151.8 s. At 11:30 London apparent time the engine's Sun is ♐17°40′04.6″, which is 6.4″ short of 17°40′11″. This is either a tabular error in White's 1823 Sun of the same size as the 1815 one (opposite sign), or Zadkiel rounding the instant (11h 30m is a round figure), or both.

Things ruled out:
- Nutation does not explain it. White's places include it: the 1815 noon Sun agrees with the engine's apparent longitude to 4.6″. Nutation in longitude was −17.7″ in 1815 and +15.6″ in 1823, so leaving it out would put the return about 13 min after the engine's, not 4.6 min before.
- ΔT does not explain it (16.4 s in 1815, about 12 s in 1823, so a few seconds at most).
- The apparent-to-mean conversion is sound. The engine's equation of time reproduces the book's own 1815 figures: 429.7 s against "7 min. 9 seconds" and 402.3 s against "6 min. 42 sec.".

The time basis is confirmed by the revolution table's Moon. At 11:30 apparent time the engine gives ♓14°12′23″, S 2°15.1′, which matches the table's ♓14°12′, dec 2°15′. At 11:30 clock time it gives ♓14°16′01″, S 2°13.5′, which does not. The engine reaches 14°12′ at 11:29:15 London apparent time. White's lunar places are good to about 0.5′ here: the engine's natal Moon is ♈5°39′31″ against the book's ♈5°39′ (p. 35).

On the clock-time reading the difference would be −152.5 s.
issues: Time basis: the return sentence does not say whether 11h 30m is apparent or clock time. I took it as London apparent time from the book's own convention (p. 31; glossary pp. 144-145), and the revolution table's Moon supports that (♓14°12′, dec 2°15′ fits 11:30 apparent, not 11:30 clock). On the clock reading the difference is −152.5 s; the 740 s tolerance covers both readings.

The birth time is Byron's 'one on the clock' (letter of 10 Dec 1821, quoted from Moore's Life of Byron), a remembered household clock time. The book treats it as mean time and adds 7m 8s. The fixture tests the source's stated input, not an independently verified birth time; the engine's natal Moon (♈5°39′31″) does match the book's ♈5°39′ (p. 35).

The place is just 'London' with no longitude. The book equates London with Greenwich (p. 33) and uses a pole of 51°32′ (p. 41). Any longitude from 0° to 0°09′W shifts both instants by up to 36 s and leaves the difference unchanged.

Use only the return instant as a fixture. The 1833 natal RAMC of 273°19′ (p. 31) leaves out the Sun's RA motion since noon (engine 273°23.0′; the 1852 printing has 273°22′). The book also erects the revolution figure with the natal RAMC (p. 124), so it is not a chart for the return instant and is not a house or angle fixture.

The revolution-table planets differ from the engine by up to 3.8′ in longitude (Venus ♏1°14′ against 1°17.8′, Jupiter ♋8°23′ against 8°25.5′), and Mercury's declination by 8.7′ (23°35′ against 23°43.7′); White's 1823 planetary places are coarse. Only the Sun and Moon matter here, and both agree: Sun dec 22°54′ against 22°53.4′, Moon as above.
This is the same worked example as the 1852 Bohn printing (previous entry). Dedupe it into one fixture carrying both citations; the only difference found is the natal RAMC.

OCR only, no doubt about the numbers. The djvu text reads 'llh. 30m.' and 'G' for ⊙ on p. 124 and garbles the p. 31 sums and the p. 125 table. Every number was checked on the page images n143 (p. 124), n144 (p. 125), n49 (p. 30), n50 (p. 31) and n53 (p. 34).

The source does not say which 1818 ephemeris it used. Pearce says he works from 'the Nautical Almanac or Zadkiel's Ephemeris' (Science of the Stars p. 120) or 'White's Ephemeris' (p. 69). His printed noon Suns for 23-24 May 1819 (p. 70) are 14.47″ and 13.29″ behind Horizons. An error in the early-19th-century solar tables is therefore the likely cause, but it cannot be proven from the source.

(b) Return step, +43.0 s. Given the source's longitude, solarReturnInstant gives 13:51:23.022Z, which is 16:21:43 Moscow time. That matches Pearce's '4h 21m' if he dropped the seconds. Of the 43 s, 24.4 s comes from the engine's Sun being 0.98″ behind Horizons in 1877. Horizons reaches ♉8°21′05″ at 13:50:58.7 UT (16:21:19 Moscow), 18.7 s after the stated minute, which is within Pearce's rounding. The engine's own error against Horizons is +60 s in total (35.6 s + 24.4 s).

The engine result also corroborates that Pearce used Urania's radical Sun: with the engine's own natal Sun the return would fall at 16:25 Moscow time.

Calendar and time basis are confirmed in four ways:
- Urania gives 'April 29 (17), 1818'.
- Its RAMC matches 10:00 LMT.
- Urania p. 44 gives Mars at '4° 33′ of Aquarius (at Greenwich mean noon)' on 24 April 1877; the engine gives ♒4°33.4′ for that N.S. date.
- The engine's Asc ♌4°41.4′ and MC ♈7°15.1′ agree with the source's ♌4°42′ and ♈7°16′.

At the engine return, Sun minus Mars is 91.27°, consistent with Pearce's square. The return carries no flags.
issues: Science of the Stars p. 124 was confirmed from the page image at the cited archive.org URL (leaf n136). The quote matches verbatim; the djvu OCR renders '4h 21m' as '45 21™', but the image is clear.

The candidate's Urania URL (Google Books QvoDAAAAQAAJ) could not be re-read: Google returned an 'unusual traffic' CAPTCHA, which I did not attempt. HathiTrust also showed a bot check. Urania pp. 41, 42 and 44 were read instead from IAPSOP's open-access PDF of Urania vol. 1 (1880), http://iapsop.com/archive/materials/urania/urania_v1_1880.pdf, at 1-based PDF pages 45, 46 and 48. That PDF is a Google scan; I could not confirm it is the same Google Books copy, but the printed pages are the same.

Nativity and return are in two publications. They are linked by Science of the Stars' explicit cross-reference '(See Urania for February, 1880, p. 41.)' and by the matching war-house cusp ♒4°42′. The Urania article is unsigned; IAPSOP lists Pearce as the journal's editor.
The natal Sun ♉8°21′5″ is printed only on the chart figure, with no restatement in running text. It is legible and agrees with the speculum (RA 35°58′, declination 14°18′N).

The title page of Science of the Stars bears no printed date. '1881' is a handwritten library note, and the Bodleian stamp reads MAR 1882. The archive.org metadata gives 1881, and internal evidence ('the late Czar'; a November 1882 revolution described in the future tense) is consistent with that.

Science of the Stars writes only 'Moscow' for the return's time basis. Mean time is assumed, and the longitude 37°35′E is taken from Urania. Whether Pearce rounded or dropped the seconds is not stated.

The source's radical Sun is 7.46″ behind JPL Horizons at the stated instant, and the 1818 ephemeris is not named. This makes up most of the +263 s whole-chain difference and cannot be bounded from the source's stated precision, which allows about ±72 s (1 minute, plus ±0.5″ ≈ ±12 s). The engine's own offsets from Horizons are +1.44″ in 1818 and −0.98″ in 1877, contributing +35.6 s and +24.4 s. Both are within the engine's documented solar accuracy.

The birth time '10 o'clock, a.m.' is a round hour from the official bulletin. Urania accepts it without rectification. This is irrelevant for reproducing Pearce, but the time is not precise as a historical fact.

verified.author: William Lilly
verified.title: Christian Astrology Modestly Treated of in Three Books (Book III, Chap. 'Of Revolutions')
verified.page: pp. 734-736 (scan leaves 768-770); natal data p. 519 (leaf 553)
verified.subject: 'our Native', an English merchant (Lilly's Book III example nativity, 'A Merchant borne the 19 of Septemb. Anno 1616')
verified.explanation:
The engine's return is 12.5 min (752 s) earlier than Lilly's. Measured against Lilly's unrounded 10h 8m 47s it is 799 s earlier. The cause is Lilly's ephemeris (Origanus) together with his whole-minute rounding.

The tables run a near-constant 7' behind the modern apparent Sun:
- Engine natal Sun at 14:33:13 UT: 186.734096°, 6°44'03" Libra. Lilly gives 6°37' Libra. Engine minus source: +7.05'.
- Engine Sun at Frankfurt noon on 19 Sep 1646 OS (11:01:48 UT): 6°19'35". Lilly reads Origanus as 6°12'. Difference: +7.59'.
- At the full Moon of Sunday 15 Sep 1616 OS (p. 506, 'about eleven' with the Sun at 2°32' Libra), the engine finds the full Moon at 11:00 UT with the Sun at 2°39'. Difference: +7.0'.
- An independent Meeus low-precision Sun gives 6°44.2' and 6°19.5', which agrees with the engine.

Because the fixture uses the engine's own natal longitude (the whole chain), the constant 7' cancels. The residual 0.54' (7.59' minus 7.05') at the Sun's 59.1'/day is 13.2 min, which is the observed difference. That residual is smaller than the source's own rounding: Lilly states that a 1' error in the Sun gives 24 minutes of error in time (p. 734). Using Lilly's 186°37' directly instead of the engine's natal Sun gives 18:05:43 UT, 184 min early: the table offset does not cancel then.

Lilly's own arithmetic was checked and is consistent: 6°37' minus 6°12' = 25'. Maginus's entry for 59'8" gives 8h 7m 2s plus 2h 1m 45s = 10h 8m 47s, stated as 10h 8m. Minus 1h 7m = 9h 1m P.M. Sidereal time 12h 26m + 9h 1m + 16m = 21h 43m, giving 23° Aquarius on the MC. The engine's daily motion, 59'08", matches Lilly's table entry.

The meridian assumptions (Frankfurt Oder, London, Frankfurt am Main) give -752, -753 and -752 s. Mixing time bases (natal clock time as apparent time with the modern equation of time, return on ephemeris time) would give -1341 s.
issues: Pages re-read on the Wellcome scan (archive.org b30338724, IIIF leaves 540, 553, 554, 768, 769, 770, 776; leaf = page + 34): p. 519 (leaf 553) natal data; p. 520 RA computation; p. 734 chapter CLXXII 'Of Revolutions' and the 31st year current; p. 735 the computation and both stated times; p. 736 figure; p. 742 natal figure; p. 506 full Moon. The quote checks verbatim on p. 735 ('comes to his true place in the Radix at Frankeford 19. September 1646. 10h 8m after noon', and later '9. 1. P. M.').

OCR errors corrected from the scan. The ABBYY text reads '3. ho. and 7. min.' on p. 519; the scan has '1. ho. and 7. min.'. It reads '6 57' for the natal Sun on p. 519 and in the p. 736 figure; the scan has a flat-topped old-style 3 (6 37), confirmed by '37. min.' on p. 520, '6. 37.' on p. 735 and the 25' difference. 'Frankgford ... ioh gm' is 'Frankeford ... 10h 8m'.

The source disagrees with itself on the birth time. The p. 519 text gives 2h 24m 25s P.M. The p. 520 RA-of-time computation uses 30 seconds (7' of the equator), and the p. 742 figure reads '2h 24. 30 P.M.'. Using 30 s moves the engine return by +5 s (difference -747 s).
The birth time was rectified by accidents: on p. 506 Lilly says the estimated time differed by no more than 1° of the ascendant. This does not affect the return chain.

The candidate's subject quote 'A Merchant borne the 19 of Septemb. Anno 1616' is not verbatim. The p. 742 figure reads 'A Merchant borne 1616, ♃ 19 Septemb. 2h 24. 30 P.M. Lat. 53'. The chapter title (p. 742) calls him an English merchant, and Lilly says the native is 'well knowne unto me'. He is a real, unnamed person. Born 1616, so certainly deceased (he would be 410 in 2026). No death date is given.

Mixed time basis in the source. For the natal houses Lilly treats the clock time as apparent solar time (RAMC = RA of the Sun + 36°07', no equation; p. 520), and he uses the same time plus 1h 07m as ephemeris time for the Sun. In the revolution he treats 9h 1m as equal time and adds a 16-minute equation to get apparent time 9h 17m. The modern equation of time on 29 Sep 1646 is about +9.8 min, so Lilly's 16 min includes his tables' constant. A fixture must put both instants on the ephemeris basis (Origanus time minus the 1h 07m reduction). Mixing bases changes the difference to -1341 s.

Lilly names only 'Frankeford' (Origanus's meridian), not the city. I assumed Frankfurt an der Oder, where Origanus taught; I did not verify this against Origanus's own title page (a web search gave only indirect support). The absolute UTC instants depend on it (Frankfurt am Main shifts both by +23.5 min); the engine-minus-stated difference does not. The fixture must convert the natal and return instants with the same offset.

Lilly's 'we dwell more Westward ... here with us' suggests his own London meridian, while the houses use the native's latitude 53°. The true London to Frankfurt (Oder) difference is 58.6 min, not 1h 07m. The birthplace longitude is unknown.
The fixture must take the natal Sun from the engine (whole chain), not the source's 6°37'. Origanus runs about 7' behind the modern apparent Sun, so the source longitude gives a return 184 min early.

The proposed tolerance covers only the source's rounding and arithmetic. It does not cover any change in Origanus's table error between 1616 and 1646, which the source alone cannot bound. Measured against the engine and a Meeus check, that change is about 0.5'.

Both instants are outside the engine's reference span (1800-2200); the results carry the flag outside-reference-span. The engine's ΔT for 1616 is 70 s ± 21 s ('reconstructed'), which shifts the Sun by about 3 arcseconds or less (negligible).

The engine return chart (Regiomontanus, 53N, 2.2W) has MC 18°20' Aquarius and Asc 26°13' Gemini. Lilly's figure has MC 23° Aquarius and Asc 0°32' Cancer: he used the 16-minute equation, a solar RA of 12h 26m and his own house tables. This is not part of the instant fixture.

verified.author: William Lilly
verified.title: Christian Astrology Modestly Treated of in Three Books (Book III, yearly judgment of the merchant's nativity)
verified.page: p. 814 (scan leaf 848)
verified.subject: the same English merchant ('our Native', born 19 Sept 1616)
verified.explanation:
The engine's return is 15.9 min (954 s) earlier than Lilly's stated time. Two causes explain it:

1. Nutation. The engine's apparent longitudes include it and 17th-century tables did not. Δψ is about +5.8" at the birth and +15.2" at the 1658 return, which moves the engine's return 228 s earlier.
2. Rounding. The remaining -726 s is about 30" of solar longitude, inside Lilly's arcminute rounding. He gives the radical Sun only to the minute (6°37' Libra, pp. 519 and 735) and takes the ephemeris noon Sun to the minute in his worked example (6°12', p. 735). By his own rule on p. 734, 1' of arc equals 24 min of time.

The large absolute errors of his tables cancel. Origanus puts the radical Sun 7'03" below the engine (6°37' against 6°44'03"), and the 1646 noon Sun 7'35" low (6°12' against 6°19'35"). Because the same kind of tables gave both the radix and the return, these errors drop out of the comparison. Using the source's 6°37' directly would put the engine's return at 15:39:26Z, 3.1 h early, so this only works as a whole-chain test.

The meridian and time-basis choices also cancel, because both instants are converted the same way. The equation of time is 9.93 min in 1616 and 9.92 min in 1658, so treating both times as apparent gives the same result.

Lilly's other timed returns for this native give engine minus stated of:
- 1646 (fully worked, Origanus plus Maginus, pp. 735-736): -752 s
- 1662 (p. 822): -479 s
- 1664 (p. 825): -295 s
- 1665 (p. 827): +52 s

With nutation removed, the residuals are -21.4 min (1646), -12.1 (1658), -12.1 (1662), -12.9 (1664) and -8.3 (1665). That near-constant offset is what a half-arcminute rounding of the radical Sun produces (±12.2 min). It points to one set of tables for 1658-1665 and to an ordinary table and rounding difference rather than an engine error.
issues: Scan checks (archive.org b30338724; Wellcome copy; London, T. Brudenell for J. Partridge and H. Blunden, 1647; Wing L2215). The quote is confirmed exactly on p. 814 (leaf 848), and a high-resolution crop leaves no OCR doubt about the digits: 'Revolutio Solis ad punctum radicis, Sept. 19. 1658. 6. 38. P.M.' p. 813 (leaf 847) confirms it is the 43rd year: 'Directions for the 43. yeer of age, beginning Septemb. 19. 1658'. p. 519 (leaf 553) confirms the nativity: elevation 53°, Thursday 19 Sept 1616, 2h 24m 25s P.M., Origanus's times reduced by 1h 7m, Sun 6 37 Libra. The archive.org OCR misreads '1. ho.' as '3. ho.' and garbles the Sun line, but the scan is clear.

The birthplace is never named. Only latitude 53° and the 1h 7m reduction from Origanus's Frankfurt (Oder) meridian are given. The 2°12'W longitude is an inference from Frankfurt (Oder)'s modern longitude, and Lilly's own geography may have differed. This does not affect the test: the difference is -953.7 s whichever meridian is used.

The 1658 heading does not restate the tables, the meridian or the equation of time. The fully worked 1646 example (pp. 734-736) uses Origanus's ephemeris and Maginus's Table of Revolutions, reduced by 1h 7m. It labels the unequated time 'Hora 9.1 P.M.' and the 'Tempus Apparens' 9h 17m, using a 16-min equation from his tables, not the modern 9.9 min. Lilly also uses the birth time unequated, both for the Sun (p. 519) and for the houses (p. 520), and sets the yearly revolutions 'without equation'. I therefore treated both instants as unequated. If 6h 38m were his equated time instead, the difference would be about +6 s. Mixing a modern-EoT apparent birth with a mean return would give about -1550 s, just outside the tolerance, but that mixing contradicts his procedure.

Lilly's absolute solar places are about 7' low against the engine. The fixture is valid only as a whole-chain test: take the natal longitude the engine computes for the stated birth instant. Never feed in the source's 6°37'; that gives a return 3.1 h early (1658-09-29T15:39:26Z).

This is a forward computation (the book was printed in 1647) from 17th-century tables that had no nutation. By Lilly's own rule and rounding the source is good only to about ±25 min, so it cannot test the engine more finely than that. Nutation alone accounts for -228 s of the difference. How far his tables drifted between 1616 and 1658 cannot be known from the text.

Both instants lie outside the engine's REFERENCE_SPAN (1800-2200), and the results are flagged 'outside-reference-span'. ΔT comes from the reconstructed segment (70.2 s ± 20.8 s at the birth); its effect on return minus birth is under a minute.

The candidate's notes are partly wrong. The 1659 heading (p. 815) gives a date only, 'beginning ☽ Sept. 19. 1659', with no time. Timed headings also appear for 1662 (p. 822: Friday 19 Sept, 5h 54m P.M.), 1664 (p. 825: Sunday 18 Sept, 17h 32m P.M.) and 1665 (p. 827: Monday 18 Sept, 23h 21m P.M.), with hours counted from noon. The yearly revolution headings for 1647-1657 give at most the year. Every weekday symbol Lilly prints matches the Julian date.

The native is unnamed. The Book III chapter title in the OCR is 'The Nativity of an English Merchant', and the merchant supplied his own life events for the rectification, so he was a real client, not a hypothetical native. He is deceased by the birth year alone: born 19 Sept 1616 (p. 519; the Table of Profections caption 'A Merchant Borne ... Anno 1616'). The source gives no death date.

verified.page: p. 822 (scan leaf 856)
verified.subject: the same English merchant (born 19 Sept 1616)
verified.explanation:
The engine's return is 8.0 minutes (-479.2 s) earlier than the stated one. In other words, Lilly's 46-year interval from birth to the 1662 return is 8.0 min longer than the engine's. His implied mean year is 365d 5h48m54.2s; the engine's on UT is 365d 5h48m43.8s, a gap of 10.4 s per year.

What does not explain it:
- The time basis. Both instants are London-meridian times without the equation of time, so the meridian and the equation cancel. Reading only the birth as apparent time would give -17.9 min.
- ΔT. It changes by only 35 s between 1616 and 1662.
- The absolute error of Lilly's tables. Origanus's radical Sun is 6.7' below the engine's at the stated birth, and his 1646 noon place (6°12', p. 735) is 7.2' below. That is a near-constant offset, and it cancels in the return chain.

What does explain it:
- Rounding to whole arcminutes. The radix (6°37') and the ephemeris noon places (p. 735 method) are given to the minute of arc. At Lilly's daily motion of 59'10", half a minute of arc is 12.2 min of time.
- How the 1662 time was produced. It equals the 'Revolutio Solis ad punctum radicis' of 1658 (6.38 P.M., p. 814) plus 4 × 5h49m, minus the 1660 leap day. The 1663 time (11.43 P.M., p. 824) adds another 5h49m. Both are checked on the scans. So the 1662 time looks like a constant annual increment rather than a fresh computation. Against the engine, the 1658 revolution is -15.9 min late by this measure, and the constant steps take back 7.9 min over four years, because the true annual interval varies by minutes with nutation and the Moon's pull on the Earth.

The rest of the series gives context. The 1646 revolution, which Lilly computes explicitly from Origanus (9h 1m P.M., p. 735), is -12.5 min. The year after, 1663, is -3.7 min. The values for 1664 (-4.9 min) and 1665 (+0.9 min) are from the OCR only.

One check supports reading 5:54 P.M. as the revolution instant. Page 823 says the degree that rose at birth now culminates in this revolution. The engine's MC at the stated instant (53°N, London meridian) is Capricorn 6°34.6', and the radical ascendant is Capricorn 6°37' (p. 711, OCR).
issues: The quote and numbers are correct on the scan. Leaf 856 is p. 822: 'Directions for the 47. yeer of age, beginning ♀ Sept. 19. 1662. 5. 54. P. M. ending Sept. 1663.' The djvu OCR garbles it as '$ Sept, 19.1662* 5.-54.'

The candidate's radical Sun of 6°37' Libra is right. The djvu OCR misreads p. 519 as '6 57' and misreads Lilly's '1. ho. and 7. min.' reduction as '3. ho.'. The scan of leaf 553 shows '☉ 6 37 ♎' and '1. ho. and 7. min.', and p. 735 repeats 'Place of the ☉ in the Radix 6. 37.'

On p. 822 the instant is labelled only as the start of the 47th year of age. The 'Revolution.' paragraph just above it on the same page judges the 46th year (1661). I identify 5:54 P.M. as the 1662 solar revolution from four things: the explicit 'Revolutio Solis ad punctum radicis' for 1658 on p. 814; the exact 5h49m yearly steps 1658 -> 1662 -> 1663 (all checked on the scans); Lilly's convention that the year of age begins at the return; and the 1662 revolution judgment on p. 823.

The 1662 time appears to be extrapolated, not freshly computed: 1658 plus four constant 5h49m increments. The tables used for 1658-1665 are not named; Origanus is named only for the radix and for the 1646 revolution (p. 735). The proposed tolerance covers the source's rounding, not any drift of those unnamed tables. The explicitly worked 1646 example on pp. 735-736 is the stronger Lilly fixture.

The time basis is an inference. Page 822 does not restate the meridian, and the birthplace is unnamed (53°N, east of London). Lilly reduces both birth and revolutions to London by 1h 7m and applies no equation of time. A fixture must put both instants on the same basis. If only one were read as apparent time, the difference would move by about 10 min (to -17.9 min, still inside the tolerance).

Do not feed the stated radical Sun (6°37') to the engine. Origanus's absolute error of about -6.7' would move the return to 15:03:13.6Z, 171.2 min early. A fixture must feed the birth instant so the engine derives its own natal Sun.
The engine flags outside-reference-span (1800-2200) on both instants. The ΔT model gives 70.2 ± 20.8 s in 1616 and 34.9 s in 1662, which is negligible against the tolerance.
The values for 1664 and 1665 in the series (Sept 18, 17h 32m and 23h 21m P.M., astronomical reckoning from noon) were read from the OCR only. They are context, not part of the fixture.
Subject: an unnamed merchant whose birth the source gives as 1616 (p. 519; p. 717's profection table, read from OCR). He is necessarily deceased, and no living-person data is involved.

verified.page: p. 824 (scan leaf 858)
verified.subject: the same English merchant (born 19 Sept 1616)
verified.explanation:
The engine's return comes 3.7 min (223 s) before Lilly's stated instant, and the gap does not depend on which meridian is assumed: -222.9 s on Lilly's 2d12'W and -222.8 s on London. That holds because the birth and the return share one time basis and the Sun has the same longitude at both, so meridian and equation-of-time choices cancel.

The residual is consistent with how the 1663 time was produced. The source was printed in 1647, so 1663 is a forward computation. Lilly's headings for 1662, 1663, 1664 and 1665 (pp. 822, 824, 825, 827, all checked on the scans) step by exactly 365 d 5 h 49 m (365.242361 d), taking the 1664 leap day into account. The natal-to-1663 interval implies 365.242296 d a year. The method behind these headings is not stated on those pages.

A fixed step cannot follow the real year-to-year variation of the Sun's return, which the engine models (lunar and planetary perturbations, nutation). The engine's returns in those years step by 5h53m16s, 5h47m48s and 5h54m47s. As a result, engine minus stated runs -8.0, -3.7, -4.9 and +0.9 min for 1662-1665.

Lilly's radix, 6d37' Libra (pp. 519 and 735, from Origanus), is 7.05' below the engine's natal Sun. Returning the engine Sun to 186d37' would land 2h55m before the stated time. So the fixture must use the engine's own natal longitude, which is also how Lilly's method works: tabular error cancels between radix and revolution.

Size of the residual: the deltaT uncertainty is about 26 s (1 sigma, combined). Rounding of the stated minute is ±30 s. Both are small next to the source's own resolution of 24 min per arcminute (p. 734).
issues: The heading on p. 824 does not restate its meridian. It is inferred from two things. First, Lilly's method on p. 735: a Frankford time from Origanus minus 1h07m gives "my true time here with us, unto which I must erect my Scheame", and p. 824 goes on to judge that year's Revolution figure. Second, internal consistency: the natal time on that basis plus a constant year reproduces the 1662-1665 headings. A Frankfurt basis fits no single year length. If the time were nevertheless Frankfurt time, engine minus stated would be about +63 min.

The 1663 instant is a projection printed in 1647. Successive headings differ by a fixed 5h49m, so it tests the engine only coarsely: the true year-to-year variation alone is plus or minus about 4 min.

The birthplace is not named. The longitude 2d12'W rests on identifying Lilly's "Frankford" (Origanus's meridian) as Frankfurt (Oder) at 14d33'E. That identification is external to Lilly's text, but it does not affect the difference.

The source's radix Sun (6d37' Lib) differs from the engine's natal Sun (6d44'03" Lib) by +7.05'. The fixture must take the engine's natal longitude; using the source radix would put the return 2h55m early.

OCR doubts in the archive.org djvu text, all resolved on the scans. p. 824: the Saturn glyph is OCR'd as 'T?' and 'P. M.' as 'P. Ai*'. The candidate's 'h' is the Saturn glyph (Saturday). p. 519: OCR has '3. ho.' where the scan reads '1. ho. and 7. min.', and '6 57' where the scan reads '6 37' (the old-style 3 resembles a 5; '6. 37.' is clear on p. 735). p. 825: OCR '17V 3 2' is '17. 32.' on the scan.
The engine flags outside-reference-span (pre-1800), and its 1616 deltaT is a reconstruction (sigma about 21 s). Both are negligible at this tolerance.

The native is unnamed. Lilly says the nativity was 'rectified by Accidents', so he is a real person. Born 1616 per p. 519, he is necessarily dead. The candidate calls him 'English'; that is not stated explicitly on the pages read, though nothing hinges on it.

verified.subject: the same English merchant (born 19 Sept 1616)
verified.explanation:
The engine finds the 1664 return 295 s (4m55s) before Lilly's stated time: 05:35:52.6Z against 05:40:47.9Z. Both times were converted the same way.

Lilly's radical Sun is 7.05' low (6°37' Libra against the engine's 6°44'03"; a low-precision Meeus check gives 6°44.2'), yet the returns agree. The 7' gap is an error in the 1647 tables. The tables Lilly used for the return are about as far off at the same season, so the error cancels along the chain. If the engine's Sun is instead returned to the source's 6°37', the result lands 176.5 min early.

The 1664 time was not solved afresh from an ephemeris. The printed year-beginnings for 1662, 1663, 1664 and 1665 each step by exactly 365d 5h49m. The 1662 time is the 1658 'Revolutio Solis ad punctum radicis' (Sept. 19, 6h38m P.M., p. 814) plus four such years. So the 1664 time is the 1658 revolution plus six mean years.

The few minutes left over are within what the source can resolve:
- Its solar places are given to the arcminute, and by its own rule (p. 734) one arcminute of the Sun's motion is 24 minutes of time.
- Seventeenth-century tables have no nutation and no lunar or planetary terms.
- The same chain's other stated returns give engine minus stated of −12.5 min (1646), −15.9 (1658), −8.0 (1662), −3.7 (1663), −4.9 (1664) and +0.9 (1665).

Time basis: Lilly fitted the natal Sun with no equation of time (p. 519). His revolution hours are also un-equated: the 1646 figure gives 'Tempus Apparens' separately, 16 min later (pp. 735-736). Converting both instants the same way therefore follows his own chain. If only the natal hour is read as apparent time, the difference becomes −893 s. His natal houses, cast as the Sun's right ascension plus the clock time, would support that reading.

The source's radix Sun, 25°40′ Scorpio, is 2′44″ (mean-time reading) or 2′08″ (apparent-time reading) behind the engine's Sun at the stated birth time. Horizons matches the engine there within 0.9″.

The source's ephemeris is poor for other bodies. The Moon in the revolution figure is at 8° Capricorn, against 12°37′ Capricorn from both the engine and Horizons at the stated instant. Natal Mercury is 16°12′ Sagittarius, against 14°51′ from the engine.
The label 'thirty seventh year current' is off by one by the usual count: the 1659 return opens the 38th year. The year 1659 and the date are explicit, so it is clear which return is meant.
The engine flags the natal instant and both returns as outside-reference-span (outside 1800 to 2200).

Citation: the archive.org item b3034119x is catalogued under a different title (Gadbury, The just and pious Scorpionist, 1677). It is a bound volume, and this 1659 tract has its title page at leaf 45, p. 5 at leaf 49, p. 13 at leaf 57, and pp. 16 and 17 at leaves 60 and 61. Cite the tract by its title and by Wing G88A, ESTC R207745 and EEBO-TCP A86045. The tract is signed 'Merlinus Verax'; the attribution to John Gadbury comes from the catalogue records.

No OCR doubt for the key numbers: the TCP transcription and the page images agree on 14h28m, 25°40′, 13h29m, 202°15′, 233°19′, 75°34′ and 1659.

The preface is dated Saturday Jan. 29, 1659 (Julian). That is 8 Feb 1659 Gregorian, which was a Saturday, so the tract was written before the 1659 revolution and before the subject's death. The death is therefore established from external references: the Royal Court of Sweden's list of monarchs (kungligaslotten.se) and English Wikipedia both give 13 February 1660, and Wikipedia gives Gothenburg.

- Two terms that 17th-century tables did not model push the other way. The Moon's perturbation of the Sun is about +6.1″ at birth (elongation 72°) and −2.8″ at the return (elongation 334°). - The stated interval, 7670 d 2h10m, is 21 years of 365d 5h 49m 03s each. The engine's interval, 7670 d 1h55m13s, is 21 years of 365d 5h 48m 21s each.

I re-read the archive.org scan. Gadbury's figure on the page printed 32 (canvas 35) reads "☉ ad Radicem, pro Anno Mortis, 1668. April 8d. 2h. P. M." The hour is 2, not 7. Three things show it. (1) The numeral is Z-shaped with a flat base; the 7 in "7h. 58′" in the same book's 1640 figure (p. 19, canvas 30) descends and has no base. (2) All twelve Regiomontanus cusps in the figure match the engine for 52°40′N at 2h00m P.M. apparent time to within about 1°: Asc ♍7, 2nd ♍28, 3rd ♎23, IC ♏29, 5th ♑11, 6th ♒14, 7th ♓7, 8th ♓28, 9th ♈23, MC ♉29, 11th ♋11, 12th ♌14. At 7h P.M. the MC would be ♌10 and the Asc ♎29. (3) The figure's Moon is at 19° ♋; the engine has 19°14′ at 2h P.M. and 21°43′ at 7h. So EEBO-TCP's "7h" is a keying error.

The engine's return is 1668-04-18T14:44:47Z, which is 2h43m P.M. apparent time at North Luffenham and 43.3 min after the stated 2h P.M. (14:01:26Z). The time conversion does not cause this: the equation of time (about +1 min) and the longitude (2.5 min) are the same in 1619 and 1668, so they cancel. The cause is the 17th-century solar tables:
- Wing's radical Sun, 29°18′18″ ♈, is 5′01″ ahead of the engine's Sun at the stated birth instant (29°13′17″). An independent Meeus formula agrees with the engine to 7″.
- The 1668 figure puts the Sun at 29°18′ at 2h P.M., 6′47″ ahead of the engine's 29°11′31″.
- The table error grew by 1′46″ between the two dates. At the Sun's 2.43′ an hour, that is the 43 min.
- Given the source's own radical longitude instead, the engine would put the return at 16:48:31Z, 2h47m after the stated time.

The source gives the time only to the hour, and its figure is cast for 2h00m. It does not name its tables or say how far they could be off. The only tolerance it supports is the ±30 min of rounding to the hour, and the engine falls outside that. The same book's 1640 revolution, stated to the minute, gives engine − stated = −888 s. So table error moves these 17th-century return times by tens of minutes in either direction.
issues: Hour digit: the scan reads '2h'. EEBO-TCP A42768 has it as '7h' and has 'Rudicem' for 'Radicem'. Using the TCP text would put the time off by about 5 h (engine − stated would be −15396.6 s). The 2 is settled by the shape of the numeral, all twelve cusps, and the Moon at 19° ♋.
The stated return is precise only to the hour (no minutes), and the source does not say whether it rounded or truncated. Its cusps show the figure was cast for 2h00m, within about 5 min.
Engine − stated = +2600.6 s (+43.3 min). That is outside the ±1800 s that the stated precision supports.

Table error: the source's radical Sun is 29°18′18″ and the engine's is 29°13′17″ (−301.2″). At the stated return time the source's Sun is 29°18′ and the engine's is 29°11′31″. The two return times agree only as far as these errors cancel. The book mentions Wing's Astronomia Instaurata, Harmonicon Coeleste and Astronomia Britannica, but does not name the tables used for this figure or bound their error.

Time basis is local apparent time. Wing's RAMC of 114°13′38″ (top of the p. 6 figure) minus the RA of his Sun gives 5h47m58s, i.e. the stated 5h48m. The equation of time from the engine is +1m05s for 19 Apr 1619 and +1m03s for 18 Apr 1668.
The source gives no longitude. I used North Luffenham at 0°37′20″W (britishlistedbuildings.co.uk). It moves both instants by the same 2m29s, so it does not change the difference.
The place of the 1668 revolution is not stated. I assumed North Luffenham; the cusps fit the stated latitude of 52°40′.
Old Style dates: 9 April 1619 is 19 April 1619 Gregorian, and 8 April 1668 is 18 April 1668. The ☿ (Wednesday) sign before 'April 8' in the 1640 figure fits: 18 April 1640 Gregorian was a Wednesday.

The pagination is irregular. The death statement (20 Sept 1668) is on the page printed 23, which is the 31st page (canvas 34); the figure is printed 32 (canvas 35). The birth text is on p. 1 (canvas 4), the nativity figure with ☉ 29.18.18 on p. 6 (canvas 9), and the 1640 revolution on the page printed 19 (canvas 30).
The engine flags the result outside-reference-span. ΔT is 67.7 ± 20.5 s for 1619 and 31.2 s for 1668, which does not matter at this precision.

The same book has a second worked example, not verified here as a candidate: 'Revolutio Solis ad punctum Radicis. 1640. ☿ April 8. 7h. 58′. P. M.' (printed p. 19, canvas 30), stated to the minute. Engine − stated = −888.3 s, and its cusps also match the engine at 7h58m P.M. It has the same table-error problem.

verified.author: attributed to John Gadbury
verified.title: The Nativity of the Most Valiant and Puissant Monarch Lewis the Fourteenth ...
verified.page: p. 27 (canvas 26)
verified.subject: Louis XIV
verified.explanation:
The engine's return comes 2 h 55.5 min (−10533 s) before the stated time. The source's tables explain the gap; the time basis does not.

1) The ephemeris. On p. 26 the author says this revolution is taken "from Argol's Ephem." At the stated instant, the engine puts the Sun at 12°52.99' Virgo, but the figure puts it at 12°42'. So that ephemeris had the Sun about 11.0' behind the engine. The figure's Venus (12°49' Vir) and Mars (12°13' Vir) are behind by a similar amount (engine: 13°03.4' and 12°24.2'). The engine's Sun reaches the source's 12°42' Virgo at 11:38:29 UT, which is 4.52 h before the stated time.

2) The radical Sun. The source's radical Sun (12°42' Vir, p. 4; RA 164°03', p. 3) is 3.88' behind the engine's natal Sun (12°45.88' Vir). The test uses the engine's own natal longitude, and that shifts the return 1.60 h later. Net effect: −4.52 + 1.60 = −2.93 h.

3) The time basis is too small to matter. Apparent versus mean time changes the result by 1.7 min. Even an unreduced eastern meridian (hypothetical) would only make the difference −2.23 h.

4) The pamphlet's other revolutions show the same kind of offset. Their tables are not named on the pages I read. The 1671 revolution on p. 23 ("horæ 23. Min. 50. P.M.") differs from the engine by −1.18 h. The 1681 revolution on p. 26 ("horæ 9. Min. 52. P.M.") differs by −1.02 h. Each figure shows the Sun at 12°42', where the engine has about 12°48.4'-12°48.8'.

So the stated minute reflects 17th-century table errors of about 6-11' of solar longitude, which is roughly 2.5-4.5 h of time. It is not minute-level precision, and the source gives no error bound for its tables.
issues: Re-read in the archive.org scan. Page (27) is canvas 26 (_0026.jp2, signature D 2). The figure's centre reads, in its own words, 'Revolutio Solis. Ad Aug. 25. horæ 4. Min. 20. P.M. 1688. Luna ad Vac. Latitud. 49.' The scan shows a doubled point after '25', which does not matter. The 1688 figure has Sun 12 42, Venus 12 49, Mars 12 13 and Saturn 23, with the 8th cusp at Virgo 9. The archive.org OCR garbles this line ('Ad Ang. 25. hore 4- Min. 20. P+M.'), so take it from the image, not the OCR.

The sentence naming the ephemeris and 'the Fiftieth year of his age, beginning 1688' is on p. (26) (canvas 25), not p. 27. By modern counting the 1688 return begins his 51st year; that is the author's own wording and does not change the instant.

The nativity data is on p. (3) (canvas 2) and the radix figure ('Natus 4 Die Septemb. 23h 3 PM 1638 S.N.', Lat 49, Sun 12:42) on p. (4) (canvas 3). The Sun's sign is shown by the figure's house cusps and by RA 164°03'; neither page spells out 'Virgo'.

Authorship: the printed title page names no author. 'By John Gadbury' is a handwritten note on this Harvard copy. The archive.org metadata and EEBO-TCP A42878 (GitHub textcreationpartnership/A42878) list Gadbury, John, 1627-1704. Cite it as attributed: [John Gadbury], The Nativity of the Most Valiant and Puissant Monarch Lewis the Fourteenth ... (London, 1680), p. 27.

The source states the time to the minute, but its tables (Argoli's ephemeris) differ from the engine's Sun by about 11' at the stated instant. The engine−source difference of −2.93 h therefore comes from the source's tables, not from rounding. An error bound for those tables cannot be derived from the source.

The source does not say whether the ephemeris time was reduced to Saint-Germain's meridian; the effect would be up to about 41 min if Argoli's tables used a meridian about 10° east, which I have not checked.
The candidate's note says this figure was computed 'unlike the other figures'. On the pages I read (pp. 23-27), only the 1688 figure names its tables, so that note is an inference.

Calendar: the dates are Julian (S.V.); the 1638 and 1688 Gregorian dates are +10 days, which matches the source's own 'September 4. S.N.'. The natal 'Aug 25, 23h 3m P.M.' counts the day from noon (astronomical day); the source itself restates it as 26 Aug, 11:03 a.m.
The engine flags the 1688 result 'outside-reference-span' (outside 1800-2200). Its ΔT for 1638 is 51.8 s (zodiacs-deltat/1), which does not matter at this scale.
