verified.author: James Blackwel
verified.title: The Nativity of Mr. Will. Lilly Astrologically performed; Shewing how he hath lived, and what Death he may probably die
verified.page: pp. 10-11 (scan canvases 15-16); natal p. 3 (canvas 8)
verified.subject: William Lilly, astrologer
verified.explanation:
I re-read the archive.org scan of Blackwel, The Nativity of Mr. Will. Lilly (London: Tho. Johnson, 1660; EEBO-TCP A76792). Canvas 0008 is p. 3, 0009 is p. 4, 0015 is p. 10 and 0016 is p. 11. The nativity, the radical Sun of 20°05' Taurus, the noon places (19°14'41" and 20°12'24"), the differences 57'43" and 7'24", the answer "3 h. 4 m.", the quote, "20 h. 50 m.", "56 mi-nutes" and the caption "20 h. 56 m. P. M." all match the candidate. Lilly is deceased: DNB 1885-1900 vol. 33 (Sidney Lee, 1893, on Wikisource) says "Lilly died of paralysis at Hersham on 9 June 1681".

The engine's return is 19.0 min earlier than the stated 20h56m London apparent time. The difference comes from the author's tables. His solar places are about 5' ahead of the engine in both years: +338" at the radix (Rudolphine Tables), and +299" and +293" at London apparent noon on 29 and 30 April 1661, against the engine's 19°09'42" and 20°07'30". That is about 2 hours of solar motion. In a return this common offset mostly cancels. What remains is the difference between his 1602 place and his 1661 places, about 42-46", or 18-19 min, which is almost the whole residual. Part of that may be the rounding of the radical place to whole minutes (±30" is about ±12.5 min). The engine's Sun is good to about 1", and ΔT changes the result by less than a minute.

The other readings give: -780 s for the printed 20h50m, -1020 s for 20h54m, -1385 s for London mean time, and -1430 s for Diseworth apparent time.

I propose no tolerance. From the source alone one can budget about ±23 min: ±12.5 min for rounding, 6 min for the spread of its printed times, about 4 min because it does not say apparent or mean time, and 0.6 min for truncation. But the largest term cannot be bounded from the source. That term is the error between its 1602 Rudolphine Sun and its unnamed 1661 ephemeris, together with the ephemeris meridian (London or Uraniborg, which shifts the time by about 51 min). Measured against the engine, that term is the whole residual. A pass at ±23 min would be partly luck, and the mean-time reading would fail it.
issues: The print gives the instant inconsistently. The p. 10 text says '20 h. 50 m. P. M.' but then '56 minutes past eight', and the arithmetic (12h - 3h4m) gives 8h56m. The printed R.A. of time on p. 11, 313°30' (RAMC 001°07', OA Asc 91°07'), equals 20h54m. The figure's MC ♈1°46' implies RAMC 1°37', which is 20h56m.

The figure caption 'April 30. 1661. 20 h. 56 m. P. M.' joins the civil date to the astronomical time, which literally means 1 May at 08:56. The text shows the intended instant is 30 April OS at 08:56 civil.
The text never states the place of the revolution. London (pole 51°32') is inferred only from the figure's cusps; the radical pole of 52°38' does not fit them.

The source does not say which tables give the 1661 noon places, nor their time basis. Apparent versus mean time is a 4m05s difference. A Uraniborg noon instead of London's would move the stated UT by about 51 min.

The source's solar longitudes are about 5' off: +5'38" at the radix and about +4'56" in 1661, worth about 2 h of motion. The 19-min agreement depends on these errors cancelling, which the source cannot vouch for. The residual differential of about 42-46" is the whole difference.
The radical Sun is printed to whole arcminutes (20°05'), which is ±12.5 min of return time. The author's interpolation of 3h4.6m is printed as 3h4m.

The source's Moon at the revolution is 4°47' Libra; the engine gives 5°43.6' Libra at the stated instant, about 57' apart. This shows large errors in the 1661 tables, though the solar test does not use the Moon.

The printed pole of 52°38' is not Diseworth's latitude (52°48'55"N per Wikipedia). The source gives no longitude, so 1°20'02"W comes from Wikipedia. The natal time is a rectified one ('given and corrected').
The TCP transcription has keying errors: 25°38' for 52°38' on p. 3, and 57′53″ for 57'43" in the rule-of-proportion line on p. 10. I used the scan readings.
The engine flags outside-reference-span for both instants (1602 and 1661), and its ΔT for those years is a reconstruction. The effect on the return is under 1 min.

verified.author: Henry Coley
verified.title: Clavis Astrologiae Elimata: or, A Key to the Whole Art of Astrology, New Filed and Polished (Chap. XXXI, Of the Revolution of the Sun to his Radical place)
verified.page: pp. 703-705 (scan canvases 772-774); exemplary geniture p. 465
verified.subject: Coley's 'Exemplary Geniture', 'a loving Friend of mine' (not named)
verified.explanation:
Re-read from the page images, all at archive.org IIIF.

Nativity (p. 456, scan 0523): born 11 March 1650 'Current', 21h 5m 8s P.M., latitude 52°18' N, 'Corrected time', Caroline Tables. The table gives Sol 1°55' Aries. The p. 465 figure (scan 0532) repeats the data.

Return (pp. 703-705, scans 0772-0774): radical Sun 12 signs 1°55'; apogee 3 signs 6°35'; anomaly 265°20', which Coley enters as 270° without the equation. The marginal table gives 20 years = 20h19m47s and 8 years = 22h31m55s. Adding the birth time 21h5m8s gives 63h56m50s; minus 48h leaves 15h56m50s P.M. on March 11, 1678 current. The p. 705 figure is 'SOL ad Radicem 1678 Curr.', 'LONDINI'.

The year is counted from 1 January. The engine reproduces Coley's natal planets for 1650: Saturn 24°03' vs 24°24' Gemini, Jupiter 8°24' vs 8°16' Scorpio, Mars 6°27' vs 6°39' Aries, Venus 21°48' vs 21°56' Pisces, Mercury 4°25' vs 4°02' Aries (both retrograde), Moon 29°26' vs 29°52' Scorpio. It does not reproduce them for 1651 (Saturn 7° Cancer, Jupiter 10° Sagittarius). The return figure matches 1678 (Jupiter 15 Pisces vs 15°29', Saturn 5 Gemini vs 5°01', Venus 7 Taurus vs 7°05'), not 1679.

The times are local apparent time. Only the apparent-time reading reproduces Coley's natal MC (15°32' Aquarius) and ascendant (22°29' vs 22°32' Gemini). At the stated time for London it also reproduces the return figure's cusps: MC Sagittarius 3 (engine 2°59.7'), 11th Sagittarius 17, 12th Capricorn 2, ascendant Aquarius 2, 2nd Aries 2, 3rd Taurus 14.

The engine's natal Sun is 1°52'32" Aries, 2.46' behind Coley's radical 1°55'. Coley's method adds a table interval to the birth time, so his absolute solar error cancels. The comparison therefore tests the engine's 28-year return interval.

Engine minus stated is -771.7 s (-770.3 s on the LMT reading; -772.2 to -771.5 s for a birth meridian anywhere from 2° W to 1° E). The diagnostic breaks it down as follows:
- -347 s: Coley's table year is 365d 5h 48m 59.4s, 12.4 s/yr longer than the mean tropical year of the epoch (365.242210 d).
- -638 s: nutation in longitude, unknown before Bradley (1748), went from -13.1" in 1650 to +13.2" in 1678.
- +263 s: the equation of centre changed by -10.8" between the two dates (apogee advance and falling eccentricity). Coley's rounding to 270° without the equation suppresses this.
- -112 s: the Earth-Moon barycentre term.
- +19 s: the engine's ΔT falls from 43.6 s to 25.0 s.
These sum to -816 s, leaving a +44 s residual from other planetary perturbations. The difference comes from the limits of the source's tables, not from the engine.
issues: Birth year: the candidate's 'born 1650/51' and 'year counted in the old reckoning' are wrong. The engine matches the p. 456 planet table for 11 March 1650 O.S. counted from 1 January, i.e. 21 March 1650 N.S. (civil 22 March, 09:05 local). In Lady Day double dating this is 1649/50, not 1650/51. 'Current' here means the year counted from 1 January. The return is 11/12 March 1678 O.S. = 22 March 1678 N.S.

Page of the nativity data: the birth text, the 52°18' N latitude, the 'Corrected time' and the Caroline Tables planet table are on p. 456 (scan 0523), not p. 465. p. 465 (scan 0532) is the natal figure, which Coley cites on p. 703 as 'Exemplary Geniture, pag. 465'. The return pages 703-705 = scans 0772-0774 are confirmed.
Quote: the print has a comma after the day, 'March 11, 1678.', where the candidate has 'March 11. 1678.'. The units are spaced in the print ('15 h. 56 m. 50 s. P. M.'). All numbers match.
Source misprint on p. 704: the intermediate sum is printed as 42h 15m 42s. 20h19m47s + 22h31m55s = 42h51m42s, and Coley's next total 63h56m50s uses 51m, so the stated return is unaffected.

OCR doubts settled by the page image: the djvu OCR reads '12 Signes, 21d, 55m' and 'against 26 years'. The image reads 1 d. 55 m. and 20 years, and the arithmetic (361°55' - 96°35' = 265°20') confirms 1°55'. The marginal table's 1- and 2-year seconds are broken in print ('5.48 .5', '11.37 5'). The 3-10, 20-70 entries are legible, and the 20- and 8-year entries Coley used are clear.

No birthplace longitude is stated. UTC conversions assume London's meridian, because Coley casts the return at London with the same clock time and makes no meridian reduction. His own precept III on p. 703 calls for one only if the place of abode is far remote from the birthplace. Engine minus stated moves by less than 0.7 s between 2° W and 1° E. The absolute UTC instants shift by 4 min per degree.
Time basis is local apparent time, supported by the natal MC and ascendant matches and the return-figure cusps. Reading the times as LMT changes engine minus stated by only 1.4 s.

Do not use the source's radical longitude in a fixture: the engine's apparent Sun reaches 1°55' Aries in 1678 at 04:51:06 UT, 47 min after the stated return. The fixture must use the engine's natal longitude for the stated birth instant, i.e. test the interval, as was done here.
The engine flags both instants 'outside-reference-span' (1800-2200). The ΔT model gives 43.6 s (σ 17 s) for 1650 and 25.0 s for 1678.
The return figure's Moon is 23 Pisces against the engine's 24°21'. This is an error in Coley's ephemeris and does not affect the solar return.
The subject is not named ('a loving Friend of mine'). The source gives no death date; death follows from the 1650 birth date (the native would be 376 in 2026). Not hypothetical.

Browser note: the shared browser pane was being used by other agents (tab-18 was navigated and its viewport emulation changed). Every screenshot used here was checked against its own URL in the tab context, and the page content confirms the scans are Coley's book.

verified.author: John Gadbury
verified.title: Genethlialogia, or, The Doctrine of Nativities (Chap. XLII, An Example of a Revolution)
verified.page: p. 267 (scan canvas 144, a two-page spread)
verified.subject: the book's example native ('the Native'), born near Oxford in 1627; not named in the passages read
verified.explanation:
I re-read the page images on archive.org: p. 267 (canvas 144), the nativity on p. 249 (canvas 135), the method on p. 210 and the table on p. 211 (canvas 116).

The stated instant does not come from computing where the Sun is. Gadbury takes the Capricorn entry for 27 years in Argoli's 'perpetual Revolutional Table' (p. 211, row 27: 13h 15m) and adds it to the birth time of 14h 26m, which is apparent solar time counted from noon. He then subtracts a 24-hour 'Day natural' and keeps the birthday date. That amounts to an interval of 9861 d 13 h 15 m, or 365.24267 days a year. The radical Sun longitude never enters the calculation. Gadbury says outright that he approves this way 'more for ease, then exactness' (p. 210).

The engine's interval is 9861 d 13 h 14 m 29.5 s, about 30 s shorter. In Oxford apparent time the engine's return falls on 31 Dec 1654 OS at 3h 40.0m P.M.; the source says 3h 41m. The date the table gave is therefore right.

Part of this close agreement is coincidence. I worked out how the result breaks down using astronomy-engine, the library the engine is built on:
- The table knows nothing of nutation, which was discovered in 1748. Nutation in longitude was −14.1″ at the birth and +12.5″ at the return. That puts the apparent return 10.5 min earlier than a return without nutation (16:03:59Z).
- Against models without nutation, the table runs early: by 4.9 min against a Keplerian Sun alone (Meeus low precision) and by about 9.3-9.9 min against the full ephemeris. Here the table's early running and the nutation shift nearly cancel.
- The Earth's monthly wobble around the Earth-Moon barycentre shifts the return by about 0.6 min.
- ΔT (σ 19.6 s in 1628, 16.6 s in 1655) and Gadbury's rounded 'circiter 8 min' equation of time each move the comparison by less than a minute.

The engine puts the natal Sun at 290.4909° (20°29.45′ Capricorn). Gadbury's radical Sun is 20°28′ Capricorn (p. 249; the revolution figure on p. 267 also shows ☉ 20 28). He read it from Origanus at a 'Tempus ultimo correctum' of 13h 23m, reached by subtracting a 1h 11m Frankfurt-Oxford meridian difference. If the engine used his 20°28′, its return would move 34.8 min earlier, to 15:19:16Z. The table method does not use that longitude, so the engine's own natal longitude gives the like-for-like test, as the task instructed.

Cross-check of the birth-time conversion: the engine's chart has MC 26°16.8′ Leo and Ascendant 10°54.4′ Scorpio, against Gadbury's MC 26°22′ Leo and Ascendant 11°1′ Scorpio (pp. 250-251). That is a difference of about 25 s of time.

Scratch scripts (no repository files touched):
- <local> (time conversions)
- <local> (breakdown)

Both run from site-r44 with node --input-type=module -e "$(cat file)".
issues: Wrong chapter in the candidate: the nativity is CHAP. XXXVIII, 'A Nativity Astrologically handled', p. 249 (canvas 135), not Chap. XXXVI. The page reads 'Citie of Oxford', not 'City'. The candidate's birth numbers themselves match the page: 1627, Decemb. 31, hor. 14 min. 26 P.M., pole elevated 51°42′.

Radical Sun now read from the page image: ☉ 20°28′ Capricorn ('Longit. Plan.', p. 249). The revolution figure on p. 267 also shows ☉ 20 28. Its centre box reads 'Schema Revolutionis ad … Dec: 31 3.41 P.M. 1654'; the middle of its second line is not fully legible.

p. 267 calls the year 'eight and thirtyeth Currant', but the computation is for the 27th revolution, i.e. the 28th year, 1654 = 1627 + 27. This scanned copy has a handwritten '28.' correction in the margin. The numbers are not affected.

The stated instant is a perpetual-table value, not a calculation of the Sun's place. Argoli's table (p. 211) works by whole signs and whole minutes, and Gadbury disclaims its exactness (p. 210). The 30 s agreement is partly coincidence: nutation alone moves the apparent return 10.5 min for this pair of years.

Time basis: the birth time is 'Tempus Astronomicum', local apparent time counted from noon, Julian calendar. Gadbury adds an 8 min equation of time to get mean time 14h 34m (p. 249). His RAMC sum, RA☉ 292°9′ + 216°30′ = 148°39′, confirms that 14h 26m means the civil time 02:26 on 1 Jan 1628 OS. The stated return inherits this apparent-time basis.

The table rule ignores where the birth falls in the leap-year cycle. Gadbury's subtraction of a 'Day natural' while keeping the date at Dec 31 happens to give the right day here; the engine also puts the return on Dec 31 1654 OS (10 Jan 1655 Gregorian). The method's date handling would not be right in general.

The source states no longitude for the birthplace, only that it was near Oxford and a Frankfurt-Oxford meridian difference of 1h 11m. That difference is applied by subtraction, and he gets 13h 23m, which may be a sign slip; it affects only his radical planetary places. I used Oxford at 1°15.5′ W. The DNB gives Wheatley, about 8 km east, which would shift the absolute UTC by about 0.5 min but not the interval.

Using Gadbury's own 8 min equation of time versus the modern −8.57 min changes the absolute UTCs by about 35 s. It barely changes the comparison: −30.3 s on Gadbury's basis, −25.5 s or −30.5 s on the modern one.

The engine flags 'outside-reference-span' (its reference span is 1800-2200). ΔT is the reconstructed model, 60.0 ± 19.6 s in 1628 and 40.2 ± 16.6 s in 1655. That uncertainty is about ±26 s on the interval, comparable to the 30 s difference, so the fixture cannot resolve anything finer than about a minute.

The engine's natal Sun is 1.45′ ahead of the source's radical Sun. Feeding in the source's radical longitude instead would move the engine's return 34.8 min earlier. A fixture should use the engine's own natal longitude, because the table method never uses the radical longitude.

The subject is not named in print. A handwritten note in this copy calls it 'Gadbury his own nativity' and mentions a tailor in Oxford named Nichols. This matches the DNB entry for John Gadbury: born at Wheatley on 31 Dec. 1627, apprenticed to Thomas Nicholls, an Oxford tailor, died near the end of March 1704.

verified.author: John Gadbury
verified.title: Genethlialogia, or, The Doctrine of Nativities (Chap. XLIII)
verified.page: p. 269 (scan canvas 145, a two-page spread)
verified.subject: the book's example native (born near Oxford, 31 Dec 1627)
verified.explanation:
The source's stated return is one calendar day late. This is an error in the source, not in the engine or the time basis.

Method: Gadbury got the time from Argol's 'perpetual Revolutional Table' (ch. XXXII, p. 211). The entry for 30 years under Capricorn is 6h43m (verified on the scan), and 14h26m + 6h43m = 21h09m. He then dated the result on the birthday, Dec 31. The table's whole days assume 7 intercalary days in 30 years. The 30 Julian years after 31 Dec 1627 contain 8 (29 Feb 1628 through 1656). So his own method puts the Sun's return on the astronomical day Dec 30 (civil Dec 31, morning).

Engine: the engine finds the return at 1658-01-10T09:16:21Z. That is Dec 30, 21h02.8m P.M. Oxford apparent time, 24h06m34s before the stated instant.

The book's own planets show the chart was cast for the later day. Its revolution places, on the second p. 270 and in the Speculum on p. 271, match the engine at the stated instant and not one day earlier:

| Body | Book | Engine, stated instant | Engine, one day earlier |
|---|---|---|---|
| Moon | Aries 19°50′ | Aries 19°48′ | Aries 7°53′ |
| Venus | Sagittarius 25°26′ | Sagittarius 25°21′ | Sagittarius 24°06′ |
| Mercury | Capricorn 21°03′ | Capricorn 20°50′ | Capricorn 19°11′ |
| Mars | Aries 28°50′ | Aries 28°56′ | Aries 28°26′ |
| Jupiter | Cancer 3°40′ R | Cancer 3°47′ R | Cancer 3°54′ R |

The engine's Moon reaches Aries 19°50′ at 09:27:05Z, 4 min after the stated instant. At that moment the Sun stood at Capricorn 21°31′, 1°01′ past its natal place.

The house cusps (MC Sagittarius 11°0′, Asc Aquarius 15°20′) were worked from the Sun's radical right ascension plus 21h09m. They therefore fit Dec 30, where the engine gives MC Sagittarius 11°00′ and Asc Aquarius 15°13′. The chart is internally inconsistent.

The same method works when the date comes out right. The 1654 entry (Dec 31, 3h41m P.M.; 27 years, table value 13h15m, 7 leap days) agrees with the engine within 26 s. Moved back one day, the 1657 time of day would agree within 6 min 10 s, the difference between the table's 10957 d 6h43m and the engine's 10957 d 6h36m45s. Moving the date, however, is a correction of the source, which the rules forbid.

Time-basis choices do not explain the gap. The equation-of-time variant, the London-versus-Oxford choice and ΔT each move the stated UTC by less than 5 min.
issues: Page citation is wrong as given. The quote is not on the page printed 269. Canvas 145 is the opening printed '269' (verso: end of ch. XLII) and '270' (recto, worn type), and the recto carries the CHAP. XLIII heading with the quote and the cusps. Canvas 146 is printed '270' and '271'. So the book skips 268 and repeats 270. The correct citation is p. 270 [i.e. 269], the right half of canvas 145. The planets' places are on the second p. 270 (canvas 146, left half) and the Speculum is on p. 271.

Quote and numbers verified exactly on the scan: 'Of the thirty first year currant of the Natives age, beginning Dec. 31. 21 hor. 9 min. P. M. 1657.' The archive.org OCR reads '21 hor. ymin.', but the image clearly reads '9 min.'

The stated return is one day late (source error; see explanation). A fixture from the literal value would need a tolerance of more than 24 h, which is useless for a solar return. Shifting it by a day would mean fixing the source. So the example is not usable.

Time basis: both the birth and the return are local apparent (sundial) time at the birthplace, in astronomical reckoning (hours from noon), Julian/Old Style calendar. On p. 249 the author adds an 8 min equation of time to 14h26m to get equal time 14h34m. The return is the radical apparent time plus the table's hours.

Natal data read from the page image (p. 249, canvas 135 right), not from OCR. The text gives '1627. Decemb. 31. hor. 14. min. 26. P. M.', near Oxford, pole elevated 51 deg. 42 min. The radical Sun is Capricorn 20°28′ (the candidate had not read the degree). The engine's natal Sun is Capricorn 20°29.5′. The engine's natal Asc is Scorpio 11°02′ and MC is Leo 26°26′; the source gives Scorpio 11°01′ (p. 251) and Leo 26°22′ (p. 250). This confirms the apparent-time reading.
The source gives no longitude. I used Oxford (1.2577 W). Wheatley would change the UT by 28 s. Erecting the return for London apparent time instead would move the stated instant by 4.5 min.

Subject is deceased. The native is unnamed in print, and was born in 1627 by the source's own data. The data match John Gadbury's own birth: the DNB entry (vol. 20, 1889, on Wikisource) gives Wheatley, Oxfordshire, 31 Dec 1627, and death near the end of March 1704. A handwritten note in the margin of p. 249 of the scanned copy says this is Gadbury's own nativity.

In the natal reduction the author subtracts the Frankfurt-Oxford meridian difference (1h11m), giving 13h23m. For a place west of Frankfurt that looks like the wrong sign. It explains part of his natal planet errors (Moon Pisces 10°52′ against the engine's Pisces 11°46′) but barely affects the radical Sun.
The Mars sign glyph on the second p. 270 is ambiguous in print. The Speculum on p. 271 puts Mars at 28°50′ in the Aries column, which matches the engine's Aries 28°56′.
The engine flags outside-reference-span for both 1628 and 1658. ΔT is about 60 s (σ 20 s) in 1628 and about 38 s (σ 16 s) in 1658, negligible against the 24 h discrepancy.

- MC 5°01' Sagittarius (figure ♐5)
- 11th cusp 18°35' Sagittarius (♐19)
- 12th cusp 4°31' Capricorn (♑4)
- Ascendant 4°55' Aquarius (♒5)
- 2nd cusp 6°21' Aries (♈6)

The natal figure also matches the engine (Moon -21', Saturn +19', Mars +4', Venus -37', Jupiter -33'), so the tables are good. Even so, a fixture would rest on an editorial correction of a printed date, which the rules forbid.

verified.explanation:
The source is internally consistent, but its solar places come from 17th-century tables, not the modern Sun. The tables are not named on pp. 45-46.

How the +201 min splits:
- Natal: at the stated birth instant the engine's Sun is 29°11.70' Sco, which is 2.70' past the source's radical 29°09'. That alone moves the return about 64 min later.
- Return: at the stated return instant the engine's Sun is 29°03.20' Sco, which is 5.80' short of the 29°09' shown in the revolution figure. The true Sun reached 29°09' only at 02:39:15 UT, 137 min after the stated instant.
- The two errors have opposite signs, so they add (64 + 137 ≈ 201 min) instead of cancelling.

How the two figures compare with the engine:
- The radical figure agrees to a few arcminutes: Moon 29°32' vs 29°40.7', Mercury 13°09' vs 13°15.4', Mars 0°48' Sag vs 0°43.3', Saturn 13°14' Vir vs 13°09.7'.
- The 1600 figure gives the planets other than the Sun only to whole degrees, and they are coarse: Moon 2° Gem vs 4°30', Mercury 21° Sco vs 25°21', Venus 11° vs 12°15' Sag, Jupiter 18° vs 19°01' Vir.
- So the 1600 solar place the author used ran about 5.8' fast.

What is not the cause:
- Time basis: both figures are cast on local apparent time, and the equation of time is nearly the same on both dates (+13.41 and +13.53 min). It cancels when applied to both alike; mixing apparent and mean time moves the result only by ±13.5 min.
- The 12-hour astronomical-day convention and the 10-day Julian-to-Gregorian shift are both applied.
- The engine: its Sun agrees with an independent Meeus solar series to 16" in 1566 and 1" in 1600.
issues: Confirmed on the scans (IIIF leaves 0071 and 0072). The p. 45 header reads 'A Collection of divers choice Nativities. 45'. Its natal box: 'Earl of Essex, born 1566. ☽ Novem. 11. 9h. 50m. P. M. Sub Lat. 52 deg.' The radical Sun '☉ 29.9.' sits in a column of planets marked ♏. The p. 46 header reads '46 Collectio Geniturarum, Or,'. Its revolution box: 'Revolution for the year of Death, 1600. Nov. 10. 12h. 35m. P. M. Sub Lat. 51 d. 32 m.', and the revolution figure also shows the Sun at 29.9. The archive.org OCR of these pages is garbled, so every number was read from the page images; the images are clear.

Subject is deceased. Page 45 says he was beheaded on February 25, Ash Wednesday, at eight in the morning. The p. 46 figure calls 1600 (Old Style year) the year of death. Checks: Julian Easter 1601 fell on 12 Apr, so Ash Wednesday was 25 Feb, and the JDN gives a Wednesday. Wikipedia (Robert Devereux, 2nd Earl of Essex) gives execution by beheading at the Tower on 25 February 1601, Julian. The text on p. 45 names the native as Robert, Earl of Essex, of Queen Elizabeth's time.

Time convention trap: '12h. 35m. P.M.' counts hours from noon, so it means civil 00:35 on 11 Nov (Julian), not 12:35 on 10 Nov. A fixture that reads it as 12:35 would be 12 h off. The figure's cusps confirm 00:35.

Engine minus stated = +12078 s (+201.3 min) on the primary reading, and +187.8 to +224.3 min across the apparent/mean and London/2.5°W variants. In every case the engine is later, and the gap is far beyond the one-hour bar.
The birth longitude is not stated; the source gives only 'Sub Lat. 52 deg.'. I assumed the London meridian. A Herefordshire meridian (2.5°W) moves the natal UT and the engine's return by +9.6 min.

The revolution figure's ASC/DSC are printed ♍21/♓21. At 51°32' that does not fit the figure's own MC ♊7; the engine gives an ASC of 12°49' Vir. Every other cusp fits 00:35 apparent time, so this is an error in the source's figure. It does not affect the return time.

The source's birth date, 1566 Nov 11, differs from Wikipedia's 10 Nov 1565 (Julian). The figure is self-consistent for 1566: the Monday glyph matches, and the Moon is just past the Sun at 29° Sco, which the engine confirms as a new moon then. So the nativity is the source's own and may not be the historical birth.
Small differences in the radical figure: Venus 1°59' Sco vs engine 2°32.9', and node 11°47' Sco vs engine node 12°58'. These are ordinary table differences.
Stated precision: the time is given to the minute, but it rests on a solar place stated only to 1' (about 24 min of time). The other revolution planets are given to whole degrees only.

verified.subject: 'The Lord Francis Villiers'
verified.explanation:
The page checks out. The IIIF crop of archive.org b30325134 (Gadbury, Collectio Geniturarum, London: James Cottrel, 1662; Wellcome copy, Public Domain Mark) is p. 50 (image _0076), headed 'Collectio Geniturarum: Or,'. Its caption matches the candidate's quote apart from spacing and a ct ligature. The figure prints ☉ 22.27 on the ♈ 8 Descendant, and the caption ends with the aspect note ☽ in □ ♀ ad △ ☉. The natal figure is on p. 49 (_0075, headed 'A Collection of divers choice Nativities.'). Its caption gives the Lord Francis Villiers, born 1629 April 1, 14h 50m P.M., latitude 51°32', and the figure prints ☉ 22.27 next to the ♈ 6 cusp, with RAMC 243.15 above it. The index lists him as nativity no. 33 on p. 49. He is dead: p. 49 says he lost his life near Kingston upon Thames on 7 July 1648, the revolution is labelled 'pro anno Mortis, 1648', and a 1648 elegy (EBBA 36657, https://ebba.english.ucsb.edu/ballad/36657/citation) is titled for his being slain by the rebels near Kingston on 7 July 1648.

Engine result (1.1.0-rc.1, pinned Node 22.22.2): natal Sun 22.345928° (22°20'45.3" ♈) against the source's radical 22°27' ♈, so the engine is 6.24' behind. The return is 1648-04-11T17:23:18.6Z, 108 s before the stated 17:25:06.7Z. At the stated instant the engine's Sun is 22°20'49.7", 4.4" past its natal Sun.

Why they differ:
- Gadbury's tables put the Sun about 6.2' ahead of the modern position in both years (+6.24' in 1629, +6.17' implied in 1648). That nearly constant offset cancels in the return.
- The 108 s left over is 4.4" of solar longitude: a small change in the tables' solar error over 19 years, and/or Gadbury's rounding.
- It is far inside the source's own precision. The radical point is printed only to the arcminute (±0.5' = ±12.3 min of solar motion) and the time only to the minute.
- Apparent versus mean time moves the difference by less than 1 s (EoT −0.725 vs −0.712 min). The London longitude moves it by 0 s.
- Nutation and the lunar inequality almost cancel, because 19 years is about one nodal cycle and one Metonic cycle. Gadbury himself notes the Moon back at her radical place.
- An independent check against JPL Horizons (DE441, apparent ecliptic of date, in TT) gives 22.3455708° at the natal TT and 22.3456737° at the engine's return TT. That puts the true return about 9 s before the engine's, so the 108 s is the source's, not the engine's.
issues: Take the natal longitude from the engine's own chart, not from the source. The source's radical ☉ 22°27' ♈ is 6.24' ahead of the engine's 22°20'45.3". Feeding 22.45° into solarReturnInstant gives 1648-04-11T19:56:42Z, 151.6 min after the stated time. The fixture works only as a whole-chain test from the stated birth instant, as the task specifies.

Time basis is inferred, not stated. Apparent time is shown by the printed RAMC 243°15' (= RA☉ + 14h50m×15°) and by every printed cusp of both figures matching within 1°. EoT is -0.7 min on both dates, so reading the times as mean time changes the difference only from -108.2 s to -108.9 s.

No longitude or place name is printed, only 'Sub Lat. 51 d. 32m.'. I assumed London at 0°06' W. The difference is invariant to this choice (-108.2 s at 0°, -0.1° and -0.127°), but the absolute UT instants shift by 4 s per arcminute of longitude.

Dates are Old Style and the natal hour is in astronomical reckoning: 1629 April 1, 14h50m P.M. is civil 2 April O.S. 02:50, or 1629-04-12 Gregorian. The return is 1648-04-11 Gregorian. The printed ☉ 22° ♈ only fits the Old Style reading.

Outside the engine's REFERENCE_SPAN (1800-2200): natalChart, solarReturn and the return chart all carry 'outside-reference-span'. ΔT comes from the SMH 2016 reconstruction: 59.0 s (σ 19.4 s) in 1629 and 44.9 s in 1648. The site clips return searches to 1800-2200 and would refuse this return, so it can only be a package fixture, expecting the flag.

The tables are not named for this figure. Elsewhere the book credits Origanus and Argol for other nativities. The 1629 positions show 17th-century table errors: Moon ♐ about 12° vs engine ♐14°04', Mars ♓9 vs ♓10°20', Mercury 0°40' (sign implied, presumably ♉) vs ♈29°02' R. So no table-based error bound is available, only the printed precision.

OCR doubt: archive.org's djvu OCR garbles both captions (e.g. '1648. April ts 5 he 24. . Pa (MM.'), so the reading rests on the page images, which are clear. The '5' in '5 h.' is the same old-style glyph as in '51 d.', and the printed return cusps (Asc ♎8, MC ♋11) are reproduced only near 17:24 apparent time, which confirms 5h 24m.
Source inconsistency, not affecting the numbers: p. 49 says he died 'aged but 18 years', but 1629 to 7 July 1648 is 19 years.

Referred to the La-titude of Birth.', with Sun 27.44 in the 3rd house.

For the stated birth instant the engine puts the Sun at 27°46.10' Scorpio, 2.10' past Gadbury's 27°44'. The engine's return comes 2h 02m 04s before Gadbury's (-7324 s). The time basis does not explain this. Both instants are converted the same way, and reading them as local mean time gives the same -122.1 min. The assumed longitude cancels too.

The whole gap comes from Gadbury's solar places, and it splits into two parts:
- In 1607 his Sun is 2.10' behind the engine's. The engine's Sun reaches 27°44' 49.8 min before the stated birth.
- In 1646, at his stated return instant, the engine's Sun is already at 27°51.25'. So his 1646 Sun was 7.25' behind; the engine reached 27°44' 171.9 min before his instant.
- Total: -171.9 + 49.8 = -122.1 min.

So his tables are inconsistent between the two epochs by 5.15' of solar longitude, about 2 h of solar motion. Pages 101-102 do not name the tables he used. A check with astronomy-engine alone (its own dT, bisection) gives -121.7 min, and the dT uncertainty is tens of seconds, so the engine is not the cause. The printed minute is nominal precision; its accuracy is limited by 17th-century tables, here to about 2 h.
issues: Accuracy of the source's tables: Gadbury's revolution is 2h 02m later than the engine's for the same nativity. His radical Sun is 2.10' behind the engine's, and his 1646 Sun is 7.25' behind. That miss is more than the one-hour bar for a meaningful solar-return test.

Pp. 101-102 do not name the tables or ephemeris. The OCR of the front matter (first 100k characters) mentions Gadbury's own solar tables and Stadius's ephemerides for other nativities, not for this one, so the tables' accuracy cannot be taken from the source.
Printed latitude 'Lat. 53 d. 32 m.' contradicts Amersham (51°40' N) and the figures' own cusps, which fit 51°32'. It is probably a misprint. It does not affect the return instant.
No longitude is stated. Amersham's 0°36.5' W was assumed; it cancels in engine minus stated.

The time basis is not stated in words. Local apparent time is inferred from the printed RAMC 221°11' and from the cusps of both figures. Equation of time is +13.86 min (1607) and +13.89 min (1646). Reading the times as mean time leaves the difference unchanged (-122.1 min).
'12h. 8m. P.M.' is astronomical reckoning (hours after noon), so the return is civil 00:08 on 10 Nov 1646 O.S. Read as 12:08 midday, the cusps would contradict the figure.
Dates are Old Style (Julian): add 10 days for Gregorian. Year 1646 is unaffected by the Lady Day new year. Death date as printed: 13 March 1646/7.
Engine flags outside-reference-span (1607 and 1646 are outside 1800-2200). Model dT is 79.6 s, sigma 21.8 s (1607), and 45.9 s (1646), which is negligible against the 2 h gap.
In the archive.org djvu text the OCR of both figure captions is garbled ('Nafe.Mt.JohnGre-', 'Revalutio Solis pro 1. aBio CMortis,16.46'). All values were read from the page images, which are clear.

Other planets at the stated return agree with the engine to within about 1.7° (Moon Aries 18 vs 19.3, Venus 5 vs Scorpio 6.7, Saturn Taurus 13 R vs 13.4 R), as expected of period tables. This does not affect the Sun test.

DNB vol. 23 (1890), Gordon Goodwin, 'Gregory, John (1607-1646)' (Wikisource): orientalist, born at Amersham on 10 Nov 1607, died 13 March 1646 [O.S.] at Kidlington near Oxford.

verified.explanation:
The source's printed natal (radix) Sun causes almost the whole difference; the engine is not at fault.

What the pages say: I re-read leaves 143-144 of archive.org b30325134 as full-resolution images, because the OCR text garbles these pages. On p.121, Judge Reeves was born 1589 Dec 24 Old Style, a little after noon, at latitude 52 deg 32'. The figure shows the Sun at 12.31 in the 9th house, beside an MC cusp of Capricorn 14, so the natal Sun is 12 deg 31' Capricorn. On p.122, the revolution is 1646 Dec 23 at 10h 20m P.M. for London's latitude, and its figure also shows the Sun at 12.31.

The 12 deg 31' is not a misprint. The directions on p.121 use it: 'Descentio Obliqua Solis 282.21' is the oblique descension of 12 deg 31' Capricorn under the Sun's stated 3 deg pole.

What the engine says: at the birth time implied by the figure (1590-01-03T12:04:43Z), the engine's natal Sun is 282.96743 deg, which is 12 deg 58.05' Capricorn. JPL Horizons gives 282.96742 deg for the same instant. So the source's natal Sun is 27.05' behind. With the engine's natal Sun, the return comes 35,391 s (+9.83 h) after the stated instant. On the mean-time reading of the clock the gap is +35,699 s. For births between noon and 12:30 apparent time it ranges from +9.76 h to +10.26 h.

Testing only the return step: the engine's return to the source's own 12 deg 31' (solarReturnInstant of 282.51667 deg) is 1647-01-02T21:38:49Z. That is 2,802 s earlier than the stated instant (2,495 s on the mean-time reading). At Gadbury's instant the engine's Sun is at 12 deg 33.0', so his 1646 tables put the Sun about 2' too low.

The two errors add up: +10.61 h from the 27' natal-Sun error, minus 0.78 h from the 1646 table error, gives +9.83 h.

Apart from that 2', the revolution figure matches the engine sky well. All cusps are within 0.9 deg, and the planets are within about 1 deg: Saturn 11 Taurus R, Jupiter 6 Leo R, Mars 11 Leo R, Venus 2 Capricorn, Mercury 2 Aquarius. The Moon (8 Sagittarius against 9 deg 23') is 1.4 deg off.

The natal figure does much worse. Compared with the engine, its Moon is +25' off, Mercury +65', Mars -40', Saturn -14', Venus -13' and Jupiter -7'. It also marks Jupiter retrograde, but Jupiter was direct, about 86 deg west of the Sun. So the natal positions came from poorer tables than the revolution, probably 16th-century ones. The source names neither set of tables.

Rigg) gives his death as 27 March 1647 and his birth as 'about 1585', not Gadbury's 1589, and does not mention Kingston. He is certainly dead: p.121 of Gadbury also reports his sudden death at Kingston upon Thames.

The difference is +290.5 s (engine minus stated) with the radical as printed, 23°15′19″. It is +44.5 s with the longitude the computation actually uses, 23°15′09″. The +290.5 s splits into three parts that add up to it:

(1) 246.1 s is an error inside the source. The printed noon value for the 16th, 23°15′27″, minus the printed radical, 23°15′19″, is 8″. The text instead uses 'only 18″ less'. At the source's own rate of 3511″ a day, 10″ is 246.1 s. Applied to 8″, the source's method gives 3m16.9s before noon, i.e. 11:56:43.1 GMT. Everything downstream is consistent with 18″: 18/3511 × 24 h = 7m22.95s; 11h40m22s − 7m23s = 11h32m59s; and the London angles at 11:52:37 UT reproduce the printed 22½° Virgo MC and 28½° Scorpio Asc. The error looks like a subtraction borrow slip (27 − 19 written as 18), but the source alone cannot say which figure is wrong.

(2) 28.1 s comes from the tables the source used. Its 1883 noon positions are 1.14″ (16 Sep) and 1.25″ (15 Sep) above DE441's apparent longitudes. Its daily motion, 3511″, agrees with DE441's 3511.1″ and the engine's 3511.2″.

(3) About 16 s is the engine's own offset: its apparent Sun is 0.66″ to 0.73″ below DE441 here. Returns implied by DE441 are 11:57:11.2 UT for 19″ (+274.2 s) and 11:53:05.2 UT for 9″ (+28.2 s).

Putting the engine's noon values into the source's rule of three reproduces the engine's instants to 0.1 s. The solver and the source's interpolation therefore agree, and the whole difference comes from the inputs.

Verdict: not usable as stated, because the stated nativity and the stated result disagree by 10″ (246 s). A fixture is possible only if the owner accepts the computation's own required longitude, 23°15′09″. On that route the engine is +44.5 s off, inside a 60 s tolerance.

Morin himself warns (p. 634) that the tables differ by nearly one degree in the Moon, about two hours of lunar motion. So the stated minute cannot test a lunar return to within a few minutes.

Neither place's longitude is stated, and the revolution was cast only 'prope Norimbergam' (near Nuremberg). Modern coordinates were used; 0.5 deg of longitude is 120 s of stated time.
The calendar is not stated. Gregorian fits: the Sun positions in both figures, and the death on 16 Nov 1632 (Lutzen, New Style).

Source precision: the radix and the revolution are both computed from the Rudolphine Tables. Morin's Moon trails the modern Moon by 11.1 min of arc at birth and 29.8 min at the revolution. His natal lunar latitude of 3 deg 34 min S compares with 3 deg 56 min S in Horizons. He himself states the tables differ by nearly 1 deg in the Moon, about 2 h of motion (p. 634).
Morin's revolution Sun (Scorpio 1 deg 26 min) trails the engine by 6.6 min of arc, while his natal Sun is 1.2 min ahead. This is plausibly a 17th-century solar-table error and is not checked further.
The engine flags outside-reference-span for 1594 and 1632. Delta-T uncertainty (+/-23 s) is negligible, about 13 arcsec of the Moon.

The candidate's checks hold. The engine puts the Moon at Pisces 20 deg 45.8 min at 12:04 local apparent time (the candidate estimated 20 deg 46 min). Death date: p. 635 says he was killed on 16 Nov 1632 at about 9 a.m., and p. 400 gives the battle of Lutzen.

verified.explanation:
The page, the quote and the printed numbers all check out. The time basis (hours from noon, apparent time, Gregorian date) is also confirmed. At 21:37:46 UT the revolution figure's other entries agree with the engine:
- Saturn 18d17' vs 18d18.5'
- Jupiter Pis 9 vs Pis 9d24'
- Venus Cap 24 vs Cap 24d59'
- Sun Sag 7d47' vs Sag 7d52'
- MC Tau 8 vs Tau 7d57'
- Asc Leo 20 vs Leo 20d35'
- The other Regiomontanus cusps agree within about 0.6 degrees.

The natal chain agrees too. Morin's Rudolphine radix on p. 612 gives Moon Pis 19d48' and the engine gives Pis 19d50.40', a difference of 2.4'. Asc, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn are within about 5'.

The 70.6 min gap comes from the revolution itself. Its figure prints the Moon at Pis 18d49'. That is 59' short of the source's own radical Moon of 19d48', or about 1h42m of lunar motion. Yet Caput IX on p. 634 says the revolution is the instant the Moon returns to its radical place in the ecliptic ("Luna redeat ad suum locum radicalem in Ecliptica"), found from the same tables as the radix. The text on p. 635 ("conjuncta partiliter" with Saturn at 18d17') shows that Morin worked with 18d49', so this is not just a printing slip in the figure.

At the stated instant the engine's Moon is at Pis 19d09.7'. That is 20.7' past the figure's Moon and 38.3' short of the radix. The gap breaks down as follows:
- The 2.4' natal difference accounts for 4.2 min.
- The remaining 38.3' accounts for 66.4 min.
- The engine's return to Morin's 19d48' falls at 22:44:10 UT (+66.4 min).
- The engine's return to the figure's own 18d49' falls at 21:01:55 UT (-35.8 min).

The cause of the inconsistency cannot be settled from the source. One possibility is that the instant was found from a different ephemeris than the Rudolphine radix: Morin cites Argoli's ephemerides on p. 634 as differing by almost a degree. Another is a computing slip. Morin himself warns on p. 634 that the lunar tables of his day differ by nearly a degree ("differentiam fere unius gradus in Lunae motu"), which he equates to nearly two hours. So the source disclaims timing to the minute.
issues: The candidate says the nativity is not given. It is given in the same book: p. 612 (leaf 694, iiif ..._0694.jp2) prints Richelieu's nativity, 8 Sep 1585, 21h34m T.A., Paris, from the Rudolphine Tables, with the Moon at Pis 19d48'. The Moon is in the 5th house, matching p. 635's 'quae fuerat in quinta radicis'. The printed Part of Fortune (Tau 3d14' = Asc + Moon - Sun) confirms the 19d48' reading.

Internal inconsistency: the revolution figure's Moon is Pis 18d49', but the source's radical Moon is Pis 19d48'. The difference is 59', about 1h42m of lunar motion, against Morin's own rule on p. 634 that the Moon returns to its radical longitude. The printed instant is therefore not a return to the source's own natal Moon.

The engine's Moon at the stated instant is Pis 19d09.7' (the candidate's rough 19d10' is confirmed). That is 20.7' past the figure's Moon and 38.3' short of the radix. The engine's full-chain return is +70.6 min, far beyond the few-minute precision a lunar-return fixture needs.
The source's own precision caveat (p. 634, Caput IX): tables differ by nearly one degree in the Moon, about two hours of time.

The natal figure's RAMC is printed '230. 58.'. Its own MC (Leo 8d31') and the stated time both imply about 131 degrees (the engine gives 131d01'), so this is apparently a misprint for 130d58'. It does not affect the return.

Other revolution-figure entries are well off the engine: Mercury is printed Sag 21 vs the engine's Sag 27d17' (about 6 degrees), and Mars Tau 1 vs Tau 2d13'. The lunar revolution's slow planets and cusps agree.

Quote check: the text is verbatim apart from two details. The stop after '1642' is unclear in the scan (comma or full stop), and an ink blot sits over the 'm' of 'Decembris'. The page number is 635 (running head 'LIBER VIGESIMUS TERTIUS'), on leaf 717. The examples are in Caput X ('Quo per effectus, vis Revolutionum Lunae ostenditur...', heading on p. 634); the method is in Caput IX on p. 634.
Subject is deceased: p. 635 states Richelieu died 4 Dec 1642, and Wikipedia's infobox gives 9 September 1585 to 4 December 1642, Paris.
The engine flags 'outside-reference-span' (1642 is outside 1800 to 2200), so it makes no accuracy claim there. That is immaterial next to the 20' to 59' table discrepancies.

At the stated 1626 instant the engine Moon is 14°05.4' against the printed 14°3', a gap of 2.4' (about 4.6 min). The close match is luck, not a measure of the source's precision. Using Morin's own radix of 14°30', the engine's return comes out +2838 s. The companion 1642 revolution of the same native (p. 637, 13 Nov 1642 11h58m T.A. Paris, also Moon 14.3) lands -7316 s from the engine's whole-chain return. At his time the engine Moon is 15°04.4'. The author gives his own precision caveat (Liber XXIII cap. IX, p. 634, leaf 716): the tables differ by nearly one degree in the Moon, nearly two hours of time. The 1626 revolution figure does not name its tables.

Companion check with the same native and radix: the 1642 revolution (p. 637, leaf 719) is stated as 13 Nov 1642 11h58m T.A. Paris, which is 23:58 LAT, EoT +15.17 min, so 1642-11-13T23:33:27Z. The engine's whole-chain return is 1642-11-13T21:31:31Z, a difference of -7316 s. At the stated time the engine Moon is 15°04.4' Leo against the printed 14°3'. The figure's Sun (21°36' Scorpio) and RAMC (48°39') are consistent with the engine; only the Moon is off.

Sensitivity to the radix: lunarReturnInstant(134.5, Morin's p. 614 radix) gives 1626-07-24T11:19:11Z (+2838 s). The printed 134.05 gives 10:27:21Z (-272 s). The engine's whole-chain natal Moon of 134.07002 gives 10:29:39.6Z (-134 s). lunarReturn(natal birth, Nantes) returns the same instant.

Engine against the nativity at the Gregorian natal instant: ASC 21°55' Libra (printed 21°54'); MC 28°04' Cancer (28); Venus 29°24.5' Leo (29°23'); Jupiter 27°02' (27°0'); Mars 19°40' Capricorn (19°42'); Mercury 2°41' Virgo R (2°54' R); Saturn 24°37' Sagittarius (24°21'); Sun 8°48' Virgo (8°42'). The engine flags both instants outside-reference-span. ΔT is 126.7 ± 25.2 s (1576) and 61.3 ± 19.7 s (1626), worth about ±40 s on the engine's UT return. That is far below the source's uncertainty.

Tronsonus' expelled from court on 2 Aug 1626 and the same man dying 8 Dec 1642. Born 1576 (p. 614), so he is long deceased and not a living person.

Possible lead, which I have not verified: p. 614 also prints Tronson's 1616 solar revolution (1616 Augusti 31. 13. 43. T.A. Parisiis, RAMC 6°5', Sun 8.42). It could serve as a solar-return candidate for P2.A.timing.returns.

verified.author: Jean-Baptiste Morin (1583-1656)
verified.title: Astrologia Gallica, Liber XXIII, Caput X (examples of lunar revolutions)
verified.page: p. 636 (intro and death date, right column) and p. 637 (figure, top). Scan leaves 718-719.
verified.subject: D. Tronson (same native as the 1626 example)
verified.explanation:
The engine's return comes 2 h 02 min (-7316 s) before Morin's, and the gap comes from Morin's lunar positions, not from the engine. The other bodies agree within minutes of arc: at the nativity, Sun 6' and Venus and Jupiter about 2'; at the return, the RAMC is within 10' and the printed cusps and Mars agree.

Where the gap comes from:
1. Natal Moon. Morin's natal figure (p. 614, cast 'Ex Tab. Rudolph.') prints the radical Moon as '☽ 14.30', i.e. 14°30' Leo. The engine's Moon at the same instant is 14°04.23' Leo, so Morin is +25.8' ahead. That alone moves the return about 52 min earlier.
2. Return Moon. At Morin's stated instant the engine's Moon is at 15°04.4' Leo, but his figure prints '☽ 14.3'. If that means the radical 14°30', his Moon is 34.4' behind (about 70 min). If it means 14°03', it is 61' behind (about 124 min). The engine reaches 14°30' Leo at 22:23:47 UT (-69.7 min) and 14°03' Leo at 21:29:05 UT (-124.4 min).

The two errors add rather than cancel. My conversion of Morin's times does not cause the gap: the RAMC, the cusps and the other planets show it is right.

A check on the same native points to a slip in Morin's 1642 lunar computation rather than a general weakness of his tables. His previous lunar revolution of Tronson (p. 636 figure: '1626. Julii D. H. M. 23. 22. 20. T.A. Nannetæ Lat. 47.', RAMC 98°24', also printing '☽ 14.3') goes through the identical chain to within 2.2 min. There, the engine's Moon at the stated instant is 14°05.4' Leo, an offset close to the natal one, so the errors cancel. The 1642 figure carries about 1° (2 h) of extra error. The source cannot tell me whether that came from his tables or ephemeris or from arithmetic, and I have not corrected any of his numbers.
issues: Unusable as a lunar-return fixture: engine minus stated is -7316 s (about -2 h 02 min, Moon about 1°). A lunar-return fixture needs agreement within a few minutes, and no tolerance that would pass can be justified from the source.

The candidate says the birth data and radical Moon are not given. That is true of pp. 636-637 only: the same book gives the nativity on p. 614 (leaf 696), 'Nativitas Illustrissimi D. Ludovici Tronsoni', with '1576. Augusti D. H. M. 31. 21. 19. T.A. Parisiis. Ex Tab. Rudolph.', RAMC 120°4' and '☽ 14.30' (14°30' Leo).

The source is internally inconsistent. Both of Tronson's lunar-revolution figures (1626 on p. 636, 1642 on p. 637) print the Moon as '☽ 14.3', but the natal figure prints '14.30'. So '14.3' is either 14°30' with the zero dropped, or 14°03', which contradicts the radical place. The candidate's '14°3'' and 'Moon to the arc-minute' are therefore not established.

The natal date is printed in the new style (Gregorian) even though 1576 predates France's change of calendar in December 1582, and the day is counted from noon. Both are confirmed by the RAMC (engine 120.17° vs 120°04') and by Venus, Jupiter and the Sun. A fixture must state this, or a Julian reading would shift the birth by 10 days.

Time basis: 'T.A.' is local apparent time, with hours counted from noon. Converting it needs the equation of time (+0.47 min in 1576, +15.15 min in 1642, from the engine's apparent Sun) and Paris longitude 2°20'14" E.
Both natal and return instants are flagged 'outside-reference-span' (1800-2200). The ΔT model sigma is about 25 s (1576) and 18 s (1642), which moves the Moon by under 15", negligible here.

Death and identity are confirmed. P. 636 reads 'obiit die 8. Decembris 1642. hora circiter nona matutina' (the book repeats the date elsewhere). The book's chapter on solar revolutions calls 1642 his 67th solar revolution, 'in qua extremum naturae fatum passus est'. Tronson was born 1576.
The candidate's rough modern check is confirmed: the engine's Moon at the stated instant is 15°04.4' Leo.

Lead, not verified beyond the figure's centre, RAMC and Moon: the 1626 lunar revolution of the same native (p. 636, Nantes) agrees with the engine chain within 2.2 min (engine 1626-07-24T10:29:43Z vs stated LAT 10:20 Nantes = 10:31:53Z). It may deserve a separate full verification, though it shares the same '14.3' versus '14.30' ambiguity.

I read all numbers from the IIIF page images (leaves 696, 718, 719). The item's OCR (djvu.txt) garbles the name ('Tronfoni', 'Tronioni') and several figure numbers, so it was used only to locate pages.
The archive.org full-text search API returned truncated (failed) responses. The shared browser pane was also in use by other agents, so every image read was checked against the tab's URL.

verified.author: Jean-Baptiste Morin (1583-1656)
verified.title: Astrologia Gallica, Liber XXIII, Caput X (examples of lunar revolutions)
verified.page: p. 636 (intro, right column bottom) and p. 637 (figure, bottom; dates of illness and death, right column). Scan leaves 718-719.
verified.subject: François de Bonne, duc de Lesdiguières, Constable of France ('invictissimi Connestabilis Desdiguiers')
verified.explanation:
The engine is 561 s later than the stated time on the whole chain, and 421.5 s later using the source's radical Moon of 17°21' Pisces. Old tables and unstated time corrections easily explain this; there is no sign of an engine fault.
(1) At the stated instant the engine's Moon is at 17°16.60' Pisces. The figure prints only '☽ 17', so the degree agrees. For Morin's minute to be exact, his tabular Moon would only need to be about 4.4' ahead of the true Moon, a normal error for 17th-century lunar tables.
(2) In the same figure Morin's Sun is 13°28' Virgo, against the engine's 13°35.08' at that instant: his tables were about 7' off even for the Sun. His RAMC of 135°17' is 5.8' below the engine's (135.38°), which follows from his lower solar RA at the same apparent time.
(3) The natal Moon comes from a different figure, p. 406, erected by Jacobus Valesius (Jacques Valois), not by Morin. Morin never states which radical Moon he used, so 17°21' is an inference. The engine's natal Moon at the stated birth time is 1.46' higher, about 2.9 min of birth time; that alone moves the return by 140 s.
(4) The figure gives apparent time (T.A.). Morin's own method (Lib. XXIII cap. V) takes a mean time from his ephemeris at the ephemeris meridian, then applies his own equation of time and his own difference of meridians. Neither value is stated, so the physical instant he meant is uncertain by minutes.
(5) The stated time is rounded to the minute.
(6) The engine reconstructs ΔT: 61 s (σ 19.7) in 1626 and 195 s in 1543. Both instants carry the outside-reference-span flag.
Consistency checks: the preceding return (engine 1626-08-09T23:53Z) has the Sun at 17°05' Leo, matching Morin's 'Sol fuit in 17 grad. ♌'. The Moon in the 1626 figure stands beside the 5th cusp at ♓ 17. Morin himself (p. 634) warns that one degree of lunar error 'unus gradus sit fere motus duarum horarum in ☽', i.e. one degree is nearly two hours.
issues: Re-read on the scans of KB copy ned-kbn-all-00004541-001 (Hague: Vlacq 1661, 874 images); every reading was taken from a page image whose URL I checked. p.636 (leaf 0718, header '636'), right column foot: 'Quinta erit revolutio ☽ præcedens obitum invictissimi Connestabilis Desdiguiers, cujus figura subsequitur' matches the candidate quote. The long s is printed 'Deſdiguiers'. p.637 (leaf 0719, header 'LIBER VIGESIMUS TERTIUS. 637'), lower figure: '1626 Septembris D. H. M. 5. 22. 2. T.A. Gratianopoli.', '135. 17.' above it, '♓ 17' on the 5th cusp with '☽ 17' beside it (no minutes), '☉ 13.28' in the upper left, MC cusp '♌ 13' and IC '♒ 13'. Right column: 'ideoque 28 Septembris 1626 mortuus est', 'Cœpit autem ægrotare die 21 Augusti', and the preceding revolution 'in qua Sol fuit in 17 grad. ♌'. Caput X (p.634, leaf 0716) is headed 'Quo per effectus, vis Revolutionum Lunæ ostenditur, in pluribus genituris'. All of this matches the candidate.

Correction to the candidate: the nativity IS given in the same work. Liber XVII (Sectio II), p.406, leaf 0488: 'Nativitas Francisci de Bonne Connestabilis Galliæ'. Figure: '1543. Martii D. H. M. 31. 20. 58. T.A. Polus 44. 40.', RAMC '333. 30.', MC '♓ 1.28', '☽ 17.21' in the 10th house (the sign is not printed; Pisces follows from the MC cusp), '☉ 20.31' (Aries). Morin says the figure was erected by Jacobus Valesius, Lesdiguières's former household member and later Treasurer General in Dauphiné, and that he predicted the death on it. The radical Moon is therefore stated, to the minute, but on a different page and by a different computer than the revolution.

The revolution example never states which radical Moon Morin used. Taking 17°21' from p.406 is an inference. Morin's chapter IX (p.634) says the revolution must be found from the same tables that gave the radical Moon, but he does not say whether he recomputed it.

Precision is limited by the source itself. The revolution figure prints the Moon only to the degree, and Morin says (Lib. XXIII cap. V) that in revolutions he writes planets and cusps only to whole degrees. In cap. IX (p.634) he says the lunar tables of celebrated astronomers, e.g. Argoli's ephemerides, differ by nearly 1°, which is nearly 2 hours of lunar motion. No tolerance tighter than about 2 h can be justified from the source, so this cannot test a lunar return to a few minutes.

Time basis: T.A. (tempus apparens) at Grenoble. The conversion to UT needs an equation of time (+1.99 min here, from the engine) and a modern longitude. Morin's own equation of time, the meridian of his tables, and his assumed Grenoble longitude are unknown, so the instant he intended carries an uncertainty of minutes that cannot be recovered from the text.

Calendars: the nativity (1543) is Julian; adding 10 days gives Gregorian 11 Apr 1543. The revolution (1626, France) is Gregorian. Both use astronomical days counted from noon, and both RAMCs confirm the morning (civil) reading.

Engine context: both dates lie outside REFERENCE_SPAN (flag outside-reference-span). ΔT is reconstructed: 61.2 s ±19.7 s in 1626 and 195.4 s in 1543. A ΔT error of 40 s moves the return by about 40 s, small next to the source's uncertainty.

Subject: François de Bonne, duc de Lesdiguières, Constable of France, deceased. The source (p.637) gives 28 Sept 1626; fr.wikipedia gives born 1 Apr 1543 at Saint-Bonnet-en-Champsaur and died 28 Sept 1626 at Valence. en.wikipedia gives 21 Sept 1626, a secondary-source discrepancy; he is dead either way.

OCR doubts: the djvu OCR garbles these passages ('Dcfdieuiers', '2 r Augusti', and no figure contents), so all numbers were read from the page images. On p.406 the Moon glyph before '17.21' is a crescent inside a ring. I read it as ☽: it differs from the Sun glyph beside it, the 1626 revolution puts ☽ at ♓ 17, and the engine gives 17°22' Pisces at the stated birth time.

verified.author: Jean-Baptiste Morin (1583-1656)
verified.title: Astrologia Gallica, Liber XXIII, Caput X (Morin's own lunar revolutions); radix in Liber XVII
verified.page: p. 638: intro top; figure top; event date mid right column. Radix: Lib. XVII p. 397. Scan leaves 720 and 479.
verified.subject: Jean-Baptiste Morin, the author himself
verified.explanation:
The scans match the candidate exactly.
- p. 638 (leaf 720; Liber XXIII by the running heads on pp. 637 and 639; the Caput X heading is on p. 634, leaf 716): the quote, '195. 20.' above the figure, the Moon at 17 in the 3rd house beside cusp Pisces 10, the Sun at 13.26 Cancer, and the event on 9 Jul 1605 at about 8:20 pm.
- Radix, p. 397 (leaf 479): '22. 20. 33. T.A.', Polus 45°25', 'Ex Tabul. Rudolph.', the Moon at 17.0' in the 12th (Pisces), RAMC 284°27'.

T.A. is apparent time, by inference: the book never expands the abbreviation. Morin's printed RAMC equals the right ascension of his own Sun plus the apparent hour angle within 1' in the radix (284°27') and in the 1612 figure on the same page (229°52'). Cap. IX (p. 634) also says the time taken from the tables is mean time, to be corrected twice before the figure is erected. The engine's natal lunar latitude, +4°56.6', matches Morin's '4.56 S.' (S = northern).

Engine natal Moon: 346.8101° (Pisces 16°48.6'). JPL Horizons gives 346.8035°. Morin's Rudolphine value is 17°0', so the engine is 11.4' lower. The whole chain returns at 17:30:32 UT, 21m16s before Morin's instant. That gap is just the natal-Moon gap divided by the Moon's speed at the return: 11.4' at 0.531' per minute is about 21.5 min. Given Morin's own 17°0' as the target, the engine returns at 17:52:00 UT, only 12 s after the stated instant (the engine's Moon at the stated instant is 16°59.89'; Horizons gives 346.993°).

So the difference comes from the error of the Rudolphine Tables in Morin's radical Moon, not from the return solver. His tabulated Sun is also off: by +7.4' at birth and -1.6' at the return. The 12 s agreement at the return is a coincidence: Morin himself (Cap. IX, p. 634) says the lunar tables of his day disagreed by 'differentiam fere unius gradus', which he equates with about two hours ('duarum horarum') of the Moon's motion.
issues: Whole-chain difference is -1276 s (-21m16s), well beyond a few minutes for a lunar return. It is entirely due to Morin's Rudolphine radical Moon (17°0') being 11.4' ahead of the engine (16°48.6') and of JPL Horizons (16°48.2').

Internal inconsistency on p. 638: with Morin's own Sun (Cancer 13°26') and 6h07m apparent time, the RAMC should be 196°21', but 195°20' is printed; that value implies 18:03 apparent. The radix and the 1612 figure obey the same rule within 1', so the 1605 figure has a slip in either the RAMC or the minutes. The stated instant is therefore uncertain by about 4 min. Its whole-degree cusps fit an RAMC between about 195°20' and 196°15' depending on rounding, which does not settle it.

Reading T.A. as apparent time is an inference from Morin's RAMC arithmetic and Cap. IX; the book does not expand 'T.A.'. Reading it as mean time gives natal 08:14:08 UT and return 17:48:08 UT, and the chain difference becomes -2012 s.

Morin does not state the longitude he used for Villefranche relative to the Rudolphine meridian. The conversions use the modern 4°43'E and the engine's equation of time (-14.1 min at birth, -3.7 min at the return). 'Francopoli' on p. 638 is taken to be his birthplace, Villefranche-sur-Saone; the figure does not say so explicitly.
Morin's pole of 45°25' differs from the true latitude of 45°59'. This affects the cusps only, not the instant.

The engine flags both dates outside-reference-span. Its reconstructed ΔT is 115±24 s for 1583 and 82±22 s for 1605, worth about 0.2' of lunar motion, which is negligible here. Engine minus Horizons (quantity 31) is +0.40' at birth and +0.33' at the return.
No OCR doubt on the numbers used; the scans are sharp. '1605' is printed in old-style figures. The radix Saturn reads 12.19 or 12.29, which does not matter here.
Morin's own caveat (Lib. XXIII Cap. IX, p. 634): lunar tables differed by nearly 1 degree, which he equates with about 2 h of lunar motion. No few-minute tolerance can be justified from the source.

verified.author: Jean-Baptiste Morin (1583-1656)
verified.title: Astrologia Gallica, Liber XXIII, Caput X (Morin's own lunar revolutions)
verified.page: p. 638 (figure, bottom) and p. 639 (intro, top left). Radix on p. 397. Scan leaves 720-721.
verified.subject: Jean-Baptiste Morin, the author
verified.explanation:
The engine's chain puts the return 18.8 min earlier than Morin's stated instant. The cause is the lunar positions from Morin's tables (the radix says "Ex Tabul. Rudolph.").

1. At the stated birth instant the engine's natal Moon is Pisces 16 48.60' (346.8101). Morin prints 17 0' (Pisces), so the engine is 11.4' behind.
2. At Morin's stated return instant the engine's Moon is Pisces 16 57.95', 2.05' short of 17 0'.
3. The Moon moves 11.95 deg/day (0.498'/min), so (-11.4' + 2.05') / 0.498 gives -18.8 min, which matches the -1127 s.
4. With Morin's own radical longitude 347 0' as the target, the engine's crossing is at 22:54:22.3Z, only +246.5 s from the stated instant. The return-epoch positions agree to about 2'. Almost the whole offset comes from Morin's radical Moon.

JPL Horizons DE441 (geocentric apparent ecliptic of date) confirms the engine:
- Natal Moon 346.80346 (engine +23.8").
- Moon at the stated return UT 346.96035 (engine +20.0").
- A DE441-only chain gives the return at about 22:31:21Z, about 8 s before the engine's.

Morin's Moon is therefore ahead of DE441 by +11.8' at the nativity and +2.4' at the return, and his Sun by +7.5' and +3.3'. Morin warns about this in the same book. In Caput IX (p. 634) he writes that the lunar tables of the best astronomers still differ by nearly one degree, and that one degree is about two hours of the Moon's motion.

Time basis: T.A. is local apparent time with days counted from noon. This is shown by the printed RAMC equalling Sun RA plus hour angle in both figures. The calendar is Gregorian (France adopted it in Dec 1582, and the printed Sun positions only fit Gregorian dates).

The cycle is the right one: the engine's previous return is 1612-04-26T14:31Z and the next is 1612-06-20T06:30Z, so this is the return immediately preceding 30 May 1612, as the text says.
issues: Verified by re-reading the IA ned-kbn-all-00004541-001 scans. p. 638 (leaf 0720), bottom figure: '229. 52.' over '1612 / May / D. H. M. / 23. 11. 16. T. A. / Aquis Sextiis. / Latit. 43.', with Moon '17. 0' and Saturn '17. 6' in the house after cusp Pisces 11 and the Sun at '2.57' (Gemini). p. 639 (leaf 0721) has the quoted 'Septima erit revolutio ... proxime antecedens diem 30 Maij 1612 ...' under the running head LIBER VIGESIMUS TERTIUS. p. 397 (leaf 0479), radix: '22. 20. 33. T.A. Francopoli Bellerocensium Polus 45. 25. Ex Tabul. Rudolph.', RAMC 284.27, Moon '17. 0''. p. 634 (leaf 0716) has the headings CAPUT IX and CAPUT X; the Septima example is inside Caput X. The archive.org OCR matches.

The sign of the radical Moon is not printed beside '17. 0''. It is inferred as Pisces from three things: the Moon sits in the 12th house (cusp Pisces 3.18 to ASC Aries 27.17), it is listed after Saturn at Pisces 12.19, and p. 639 names Jupiter as lord of Saturn and the Moon. DE441 agrees (Pisces 16 48.2').

The printed house cusps of the 1612 figure do not match the printed RAMC 229 52. The cusps are MC Sco 21, XI Sag 9, XII Sag 28, ASC Cap 25, II Pis 11, III Ari 25. RAMC 229 52 at latitude 43 gives MC Sco 22 15-17' and ASC Cap 27 02' (the engine gives the same at the stated instant). The printed cusps fit RAMC of about 228 33', which is about 5.3 min of time earlier. The time, RAMC and Sun agree with each other, so the stated time was used. This 'clean example' (the candidate's wording) still has a possible ambiguity of about 5 min (about 2.6' of Moon).

The source's accuracy is set by its tables, not by its printed precision. Rounding alone (time to 1 min, Moon to 1', natal time to 1 min) allows only about +-2 min. The engine differs by 18.8 min because Morin's Rudolphine Moon is 11.8' off DE441 at the nativity.

Morin's latitudes are rounded or off: 'Latit. 43' for Aix (actually 43 31.6'N) and 'Polus 45. 25' for Villefranche (actually 45 59'N). These change the cusps only. Morin's longitude difference between Aix and Uraniborg (the Rudolphine meridian) is not stated, and any error in it shifts his local time against UT.

Both dates are outside the engine's REFERENCE_SPAN, and the results carry the flag 'outside-reference-span'. The engine's Delta T is 115.2 s (sigma 24.5) in 1583 and 74.6 s (sigma 21.3) in 1612. That uncertainty is small here: about 20" of Moon, which is under a minute of time.

The candidate's Moon at the stated time ('about 16 58' Pisces') is confirmed: the engine gives 16 57.95' and DE441 gives 16 57.6'. The note 'A clean example' overstates it, because of the cusp inconsistency and the 19-min chain offset that comes from the tables.

The subject is the author, Jean-Baptiste Morin, who died in Paris on 6 November 1656. Source: MacTutor History of Mathematics (St Andrews), biography 'Jean-Baptiste Morin' (https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Morin_Jean-Baptiste.html), Quick Info: born 23 February 1583, Villefranche, Beaujolais; died 6 November 1656, Paris. The 1661 Hague edition is posthumous.

verified.explanation: Almost the whole −22.2 min comes from the source's radical Moon. On p. 397 Morin computed his radix 'Ex Tabul. Rudolph.' and put the Moon at ♓17°0'. At the stated birth instant the engine has the Moon at ♓16°48.60' (346.81008°), which is 11.4' behind. JPL Horizons gives ♓16°48.21', so the gap is the tables' error, not the engine's. Morin's cap. IX (p. 634) says a revolution is computed with the same tables as the radix, to the radical place in the ecliptic. So his return is the instant his tabular Moon reached 17°0'. At his stated instant the engine Moon is at ♓16°59.55', only 0.45' short, and it reaches 17°0' 54 s later. In other words, the Rudolphine Moon was nearly exact in April 1613 but about 11' fast in February 1583. The engine's own natal longitude is 10.95' behind where the Moon stands at Morin's instant. At 0.494'/min that puts the engine's return 22.2 min earlier, at 10:52:39 UT. Horizons does the same chain to 10:52:29 UT, about 10 s from the engine. The time bases are not the cause: both conversions from local apparent time agree with Horizons' solar hour angles to under a second. The source is internally consistent. At the stated instant the engine's Regiomontanus cusps at latitude 43° match all twelve printed cusps to the degree. His RAMCs (284°27', 18°53') sit 6.7' and 5.6' above the engine's. That is explained by his Rudolphine Sun running about 7' ahead of modern at both dates: ♓4°19'18" against ♓4°11.86', and ♈26°35' against ♈26°27.92'. The engine and Horizons agree on the Sun to within 2". Morin himself, in cap. IX, warns that the lunar tables of his day disagreed by almost a degree, which he equates with almost two hours of the Moon's motion.
issues: Whole-chain result: the engine returns 1329.7 s (22.2 min) before Morin's stated instant. That is far beyond the source's minute precision and beyond 'a few minutes' for a lunar return. The cause is the Rudolphine radical Moon: ♓17°0' against engine ♓16°48.60' and Horizons ♓16°48.21', a difference of −11.4'.

The only tolerance the source itself supports is Morin's cap. IX statement (p. 634, leaf 716): lunar tables disagree by nearly 1°, almost 2 h of the Moon's motion. A ±2 h tolerance is far too loose to test a lunar return, so the example is not usable as a fixture.

Diagnostic, not the whole chain: lunarReturnInstant(347.0) falls 54.1 s after the stated instant. That agreement depends on the Rudolphine Moon happening to be nearly exact in 1613. The source does not establish it, so it cannot justify a minute-level tolerance either.

Quote and page check against the scan, all confirmed. P. 639 (leaf 721, running head LIBER VIGESIMUS TERTIUS) opens the passage in the right column, with the figure mid-page. The figure reads '1613 Aprilis D. H. M. 15. 23. 37. T.A. Aquis Sextiis.' with '18. 53.' above it. The Moon '17' sits in house 8, between cusp 8 at ♒27 and cusp 9 at ♓20, so it is ♓17. The Sun is ♈26°35'. Cusps: ♌5 ♌27 ♍20 ♎20 ♐1 ♑8 ♒5 ♒27 ♓20 ♈20 ♊1 ♋8. Caput X starts on p. 634, and no other chapter heading appears on pp. 635-639.

Typography only: in the print the 'r' of 'revolutio' is a damaged letter, the year is spaced '16 13', and the sentence ends with a comma. The archive.org OCR of this page is garbled and does not include the figure, so every value was read from full-resolution IIIF images of leaves 479, 489, 716 and 721.

Radix check: p. 397 (leaf 479, Liber XVII) reads '1583. Februarii D. H. M. 22. 20. 33. T.A.' and continues with Francopoli Bellerocensium, Polus 45°25', Ex Tabul. Rudolph., with RAMC 284°27' above the figure. The Moon is printed '17.0'' in the 12th house, which runs from ♓3°18' to ♈27°17'. Pisces is confirmed by the revolution figure and by the engine. The candidate's natal quote leaves out 'Ex Tabul. Rudolph.'.
The revolution figure gives the Moon only to the degree. The arcminute value, a round 17°0', comes from the radix.
Moon latitude table on p. 397: '☽ 4. 56. S.'. Here S means Septentrionalis, i.e. north. The engine gives +4.943° and Horizons +4.942°, so they agree.

Morin's longitudes are imperfect. On p. 407 he adds 28 min for the difference of meridians, but Uraniborg, the Rudolphine meridian, is about 32 min east of Villefranche. His value for Aix is not printed, so the stated apparent time at Aix may carry an unknown conversion error of a few minutes.
The 'Polus 45. 25.' for Villefranche is about 34' south of its true 45°59'. 'Bellerocensium' on p. 397 is a misprint: p. 407 prints 'Belliocensium'. Neither affects the Moon or the return instant.
The engine flags outside-reference-span for both 1583 and 1613. Engine ΔT is 115 s and 74 s, against Horizons' 138 s and 90 s. The effect on the chain is about 10 s.
Calendar: Gregorian, adopted in France in December 1582. The Sun positions on both dates confirm it.

Subject has died. The same volume's front matter, 'Joannis Baptistae Morini Vita', p. XX (leaf 44, §CIV), records his death on Monday 6 November 1656 at 2 a.m. Wikipedia gives 6 Nov 1656, Paris, and that date was a Monday.
