verified.explanation:
The -9.6 day gap comes from a misprint in the source, not from the engine. At the printed instant (27 Jun 1615, 01:04 UT) the engine puts the Moon at 15°06' Cancer, 118° away from the radix Moon. The nearest returns are 17 Jun 10:30 UT and 14 Jul 18:39 UT.

The figure's own contents belong to 17 June, late morning:
- Sun: printed ☉ 25.39 Gemini. Engine: 25°37.7' Gemini on 17 Jun about 11 UT, but 4°46' Cancer at the printed instant.
- Sun position: it sits in the 10th house beside MC ♊ 15, which fits a chart cast near 11 a.m., not 1 a.m.
- Moon: printed 17, on the 7th cusp ♓ 18.
- Jupiter 18 (Scorpio) and Saturn 25 (Aries): engine has 18°11' Scorpio and 24°22' Aries on 17 June.

In this book the number above each figure is the RAMC. The radix's 284.27 is worked out on p. 407. Here, MC 15°0' Gemini and Asc 18 Virgo at latitude 51 need RAMC 73°42'. So the printed '37. 42' is probably transposed. RAMC 73°42' implies T.A. about 16d 23h 14m (civil 17 June, about 11:14). That means a simple day/hour digit swap still leaves the minutes wrong.

The Wellcome copy (archive.org b33550542, leaf 718) prints the same values. I found no errata list.

Diagnostic only, not a source number: the engine's natal Moon is 16°48.60' Pisces, 11.4' short of Morin's 17°0' (Rudolphine Tables). Its June return falls at 10:37.9 local apparent time (LAT) at Calais, 32 to 36 min before the 11:10 to 11:14 LAT the figure implies. A return to Morin's 347°0' falls at 10:58.2 LAT, 12 to 16 min before. Morin's own Sun (4°19'18" against the engine's 4°11.9') and his radix RAMC (284°27' against 284.34°) agree with the apparent-time conversion. Using any of these readings would mean replacing printed digits, which the rules forbid.
issues: The printed instant is not a lunar return. At civil 27 Jun 1615 01:10 LAT Calais (01:04:29 UT) the engine Moon is at 15°06' Cancer. The returns to the natal Moon are 1615-06-17T10:30:21Z and 1615-07-14T18:38:49Z.

The figure contradicts its own printed day and hour. Printed ☉ 25°39' Gemini matches 17 June (engine 25°37.7'), not 27 June (engine 4°46' Cancer). The Sun is in the 10th house next to MC ♊ 15, so the chart is cast near 11 a.m., not 1 a.m.

The RAMC printed above the figure, '37. 42', does not fit the cusps. MC ♊ 15 with Asc ♍ 18 at latitude 51 needs 73°42' (probably transposed digits). That RAMC implies T.A. of about 23h14m on 16 June, which also contradicts the printed minutes '10'.
The Ascendant is printed '♍ 8', while the opposite 7th cusp reads '♓ 18'.
Correction to the candidate: the Moon ('☽ 17') sits beside the 7th cusp '♓ 18', not '♓ 10'. ♈ 10 is the 8th cusp. Morin's text puts the Moon 'in cuspide septima'.

These are edition misprints, not damage to one copy: the Wellcome Library copy (archive.org b33550542, leaf 718) prints the same '26. 13. 10.' and '37. 42'. No errata list was found; the KB copy's full text ends at FINIS on p. 784.

Natal longitude: the engine gives 16°48.60' Pisces (346.810°); the radix gives 17°0' Pisces. The difference is -11.4', about 20 min of lunar motion. The radix Moon latitude '4. 56. S.' (S = septentrionalis, north) matches the engine's +4°56.6'.
Time basis: 'T.A.' = tempore apparente, as Morin glosses it for the nativity on p. 407 (scan leaf 489). The EoT is -14.1 min at the birth and -1.9 min in late June 1615.

Neither place's longitude is printed; I used modern values (Villefranche-sur-Saône 4.7186°E, Calais 1.8587°E). The printed latitude of Villefranche, 45°25', is 34' below the modern value; this affects houses only.
Engine flag 'outside-reference-span': both 1583 and 1615 fall outside 1800-2200. ΔT in 1583 is 115 ± 24 s, which moves the Moon by about 13" at most, so it is negligible here.
Subject has died. The Vita in this edition (p. XX, scan leaf 44) records his death on Monday 6 November 1656 at the second hour after midnight. Leaf 45 prints his epitaph.

verified.author: Jean-Baptiste Morin (1583-1656)
verified.title: Astrologia Gallica, Liber XXIII, Caput X (Morin's own lunar revolutions)
verified.page: p. 640: intro right column; figure bottom. Scan leaf 722.
verified.subject: Jean-Baptiste Morin, the author
verified.explanation:
The time basis checks out. Run at the converted stated instant, the engine reproduces the figure's own cusps and Sun:
- Asc 19°38′ ♋ (figure ♋ 19)
- MC 22°22′ ♓ (figure ♓ 22)
- 2nd 9°37′ ♌ (figure ♌ 9)
- 11th 2°35′ ♉ (figure ♉ 2)
- Sun 3°40′ ♑ (figure ☉ 3°43′)
So apparent time, the noon-based day, the Gregorian date and the Nuremberg location all agree.

The Moon does not agree. At the stated instant the engine Moon is 15°46′03″ ♓. That is 1°02.5′ short of the engine's natal Moon (16°48′36″ ♓) and 1°14′ short of Morin's radix Moon of 17°0′ ♓. At 0.581°/h that shortfall makes the engine's return 1h47m46s later than the stated one (+6466 s). Using the source's 17°0′ instead gives +7645 s.

Morin found his return instant by moving his tabular Moon back to his tabular radix. His tables put the Moon about 11′ ahead of the modern position at birth (radix 'Ex Tabul. Rudolph.') but about 1°14′ ahead at the 1615 return. The difference between those two errors (about 1°) is the gap.

Morin warns of exactly this on p. 634 (XXIII.9). He says leading astronomers' lunar places still differ by nearly a degree, 'unus gradus sit fere motus duarum horarum in ☽' (one degree is nearly two hours of the Moon's motion), so revolution figures carry that error.

The other explanations are each too small:
- ΔT sigma: about 21 s.
- Reading T.A. as mean time: gives +5650 s.
- Morin's own natal reduction: gives +6278 s.
- Longitude choices: a few minutes.

So the 1.8 h difference comes from the source's lunar tables, not from the engine or the time conversion.
issues: The scans confirm the candidate exactly (archive.org IIIF, KB copy ned-kbn-all-00004541-001). p. 640 (leaf 722), right column, has the quoted sentence word for word ('Decima erit revolutio ☽ ... horâ prima, cum 30 circiter minutis'). The figure at the bottom reads '1615 Decembris D. H. M. 25. 5. 16. T.A. Noribergæ Lat. 49.', with ☽ 17 beside the cusp ♓ 22. The p. 397 radix (leaf 479) reads '1583 Februarii D. H. M. 22. 20. 33. T.A. Francopoli Bellerocensium Polus 45. 25. Ex Tabul. Rudolph.', with ☽ 17. 0′ and RAMC 284. 27. The candidate's quote joins text and figure with an ellipsis and stays under 40 words.

Precision is too coarse for a lunar-return fixture. The author himself (XXIII.9, p. 634, leaf 716) says lunar tables still differ by nearly 1°, which he equates with nearly 2 h in a revolution figure. The measured gap of +6466 s is of that size, so any defensible tolerance (hours) cannot test the engine to the minutes a lunar return needs.

The return figure gives the Moon only to the degree ('☽ 17'), and it equals the radix by construction, so it is not an independent check. The return time is printed to the minute but derives from tables whose Moon was about 1°14′ off at that date (engine 15°46′03″ ♓ at the stated instant).

Radix Moon: source 17°0′ against engine 16°48′36″ ♓, so the source is 11.4′ ahead. The engine's natal Moon latitude, 4°56′ N, matches the radix latitude table, which reads '☽ 4. 56' (the N/S letter was not fully legible). Neither figure prints a sign glyph next to the Moon. Pisces follows from house context (12th house, ♓ 3°18′ to ♈ 27°17′, listed after ☉ 4°19′18″ ♓, ♃ 4°45′ and ♄ 12°19′) and from the engine.

The figure above the 10th-revolution chart reads '331. 11.'. On the radix figure the matching number (284°27′) is the RAMC, as p. 407 explains. Read as an RAMC, 331°11′ contradicts the printed time and the figure's own cusps, which both imply about 353°. It is unexplained: either a misprint or a different quantity. The cusps and the time agree with each other and with the engine, so the stated instant was not changed.

The revolution figure does not name its tables (the radix is from the Rudolphine Tables). In it, Venus (♀ 16) is 2.6° from the engine's 13°21′ ♐ (retrograde). The Sun, Saturn, Jupiter, Mercury and Mars agree with the engine to within about 1°.

Place spelling on the radix figure is 'Bellerocensium' (p. 407 has 'Belliocensium'), most likely a misprint for Bellojocensium (Villefranche-en-Beaujolais). The printed pole of 45°25′ differs from the modern 45°59′. Neither longitude is stated, so modern longitudes were used for the time conversion.

Calendar: Gregorian, confirmed by the figure's Sun and cusps. On Julian 25 Dec (Gregorian 4 Jan 1616) the Moon would be about 130° away. Nuremberg's civil Julian calendar does not apply to Morin's dating.
Both epochs are outside the engine's 1800-2200 reference span (flag 'outside-reference-span'). The engine uses ΔT model segment 'reconstructed', with sigma 21-24 s, which is negligible here.

Death: Morin died 6 Nov 1656 in Paris (born 23 Feb 1583, Villefranche), per the 'Quick Info' of the MacTutor biography (https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Morin_Jean-Baptiste.html). Astrologia Gallica (1661) is posthumous.

verified.title: Astrologia Gallica, Liber XXIII, Caput X (Morin's own lunar revolutions)
verified.page: p. 641: intro top of right column; figure mid-page. Scan leaf 723.
verified.subject: Jean-Baptiste Morin, the author
verified.explanation:
The engine's return is 634.6 s (10.6 min) before Morin's stated instant. The gap comes from the source's tables, not from the time conversion.

Time basis. The source settles it. On p. 407 Morin says the radix time is apparent time, computed with the Rudolphine Tables, and he adds 28 min for the meridian difference and 15 min for the equation of time, giving 21h16m. The engine at the converted instants gives RAMC 227°01.8' for the return (printed 227°0'). For the radix it gives 284°20.3' (printed 284°27'); that 6.7' gap is exactly Morin's Sun right ascension 336°12' against the engine's 336°05.3'.

The Moon. Morin's radical Moon ♓17°0' is 11.4' ahead of the engine's ♓16°48'36" for the stated birth instant. At the stated return instant the engine's Moon is ♓16°53'54", 6.1' short of ♓17°0'. So the engine's Moon passes its own natal longitude 5.3' earlier, which is 10.6 min at 12.03°/day. If the engine's Moon is returned to Morin's own 347°0' instead, the instant is 19:55:17.9Z, 12.2 min after the stated time.

The source's Sun shows the same kind of table error: ♓4°19'18" against the engine's ♓4°11'52" (+7.4') in 1583, and ♋18°28' against ♋18°29.3' (-1.3') in 1629.

Morin's own longitudes move the comparison by only about 1-5 min. On p. 407 he puts Villefranche 28 min of time from Uraniborg; the true figure is about 32. The Liber XXIII OCR puts Paris 12 min west of Villefranche (true 9.5) and Uraniborg 40 min east of Paris (true 41.4). Allowing for these, his table Moon still runs about +13' at birth and +6' at the return.

The engine itself is checked against JPL Horizons (DE441). Its Moon is +23.8" (1583) and +19.4" (1629) from DE441, so a DE441-based return falls only about 9 s before the engine's. Morin's printed lunar latitude, 4°56' north ('S.' = septentrionalis), matches DE441's +4.942°.
issues: Death evidence (not a defect): the 1661 edition's own 'Joannis Baptistæ Morini Vita', p. XX (scan leaf 44, marginal §CIV), records his death on Monday 6 November 1656, the second hour after midnight. 6 Nov 1656 Gregorian was a Monday. Wikipedia ('Jean-Baptiste Morin (mathematician)') gives 23 Feb 1583 - 6 Nov 1656.

Locations verified on the scan. Return: p. 641 = leaf 723, right column, second paragraph; the figure is mid-page under '227. 0.'. Radix: p. 397 = leaf 479, second figure, '284. 27.', 'Ex Tabul. Rudolph.'. Time-basis text: p. 407 = leaf 489, Liber XVII, Caput V.

The djvu.txt OCR reads 'die 5 Augusti'. The scan shows the same old-style 3 as in 'Ludovico 13', so the text is 'die 3 Augusti'. The event date is not used in any computation; Wikipedia dates the appointment to 1630.

Neither figure prints the Moon's sign. The radix has '☽ 17. 0'' in a 12th house running from ♓3°18' to Asc ♈27°17'. The return figure has '☽ 17' in a 2nd house running from ♓6 to ♈24. Pisces follows from the prenatal new moon on p. 397, at ♓3°22' on 21 Feb 21h43m T.A., 22h50m before birth. The engine and DE441 also put the Moon at ♓16°48'.
Precision as printed: the return figure gives the Moon to the whole degree only; the radix Moon is given to 1' and the return time to 1 min.

Neither page gives a longitude for Villefranche or Paris, so modern coordinates were used. Morin's own meridian figures differ: 28 min from Villefranche to Uraniborg on p. 407 (true about 32), and, from the Liber XXIII OCR only, Paris 12 min west of Villefranche (true 9.5) and Uraniborg 40 min east of Paris (true 41.4).
Morin's latitude for Villefranche, 'Polus 45. 25.', is 34' south of the true 45°59'. This affects only the houses.

Both instants were computed from the Rudolphine Tables, and the source states no accuracy for them. Its radix Moon is 11.4' and its radix Sun 7.4' from the engine; DE441 agrees with the engine to within 24".

The engine read 1583 and 1629 outside its 1800-2200 reference span (flag outside-reference-span), and calc() and houses() refuse such instants. The apparent-time conversion therefore used natalChart()'s MC with meanObliquity, cross-checked with Meeus to within 0.4 s.

Not usable as a fixture. The 10.6 min gap is wider than the few-minute bar for a lunar return. The tolerance the source's own rounding supports (about ±2 min) is failed. The whole-degree Moon in the figure (about ±60 min) is too loose to test anything.

verified.subject: Jean-Baptiste Morin, the author
verified.explanation:
The scans match the candidate. Morin, Astrologia Gallica (The Hague: Vlacq, 1661), Lib. XXIII, Caput X ("vis Revolutionum Lunae ostenditur, in pluribus genituris", which begins on p. 634). On p. 642 (scan leaf 724) the twelfth example reads "Duodecimae erit revolutio [Moon] qua durante publice demonstravi, coram 8 Commissariis & plusquam 300 Viris ... Scientiam longitudinum". The figure reads "1634 Martii D. H. M. 27. 3. 20. T.A. Parisiis" with RAMC "56. 23.". It places "[Moon] 17" in the 7th house between cusps Pisces 6 and Pisces 28 (so 17 Pisces), with the Sun at 6.56 Aries. The radix on p. 397 (leaf 479) gives the Moon at "17.0'" Pisces, the Sun at 4.19.18 Pisces, and RAMC 284.27. Engine natal Moon: 16d48m36.5s Pisces (346.81013), against the source's 17d00m, so engine minus source is -11.4'.

The engine's full chain gives the return 441.6 s (7m22s) after Morin's stated instant. That is 15:27:22 apparent time at Paris against his 15:20. The gap comes from Morin's tables, not from the engine:
- He cast the radix "Ex Tabul. Rudolph.". His method chapter (Caput IX, p. 634) says the return is to be found from the same tables as the radical place, as a mean time that is then corrected.
- The Rudolphine Moon is +11.4' ahead of the engine at birth. At the stated return it is +15.9' ahead: the engine Moon at 15:16:02 UT is 16d44m04s Pisces, against Morin's 17d00m.
- The net differential error is +4.55'. At the Moon's 14.82 deg/day (0.617'/min) that is 7.4 min, which is the whole difference.
- A return to Morin's own radical 17d00m would fall at 15:41:50 UT, 25.8 min after his instant.

The comparison is independent of the engine. JPL Horizons (DE441) Moon longitudes are 346.80352 at birth and 346.72771 at the stated instant, 0.40' from the engine at both. Horizons' Moon at the engine's return instant is 346.80344, within 0.0001 deg of its own natal value. So DE441 run through the same chain lands within about 1 s of the engine.

The time reading is also confirmed by the figures' own RAMCs:
- Return: the engine RAMC at the converted instant is 56d22.2', against the source's 56d23'.
- Radix: the engine gives 284d20.4' against 284d27'. That 6.6' gap matches Morin's natal Sun sitting 7.4' ahead of the true Sun in right ascension terms.

Morin himself warns (p. 634) that astronomers' lunar tables differed by "fere unius gradus" in the Moon's motion, nearly two hours of time in a lunar return.
issues: The only tolerance the source supports is about 2 h: Morin says (Caput IX, p. 634, leaf 716) lunar tables of his day differ by almost one degree, "unus gradus sit fere motus duarum horarum in [Moon]". That is far too loose for a lunar-return fixture, which needs minutes.

The 441.6 s agreement is partial cancellation of two Rudolphine-table errors (+11.4' at birth, +15.9' at the return, measured against the engine and DE441). It is not a property of the engine, and it cannot be predicted from the source.

The return figure gives the Moon only to the whole degree ("[Moon] 17", Pisces by the 7th and 8th cusps). That the return was cast to exactly 17d00m rests on the radix (p. 397) and the method chapter, not on the figure.

The 1634 figure does not name its tables. Morin's 1634 Sun (6d56m Aries) is 0.5' from the engine, while his 1583 natal Sun (4d19m18s Pisces) is 7.4' ahead of it, so it cannot be confirmed from the page that both charts came from the same tables. Caput IX says they should.

OCR doubts: the djvu text reads the RAMC as "56. 25." and the ordinal as "Duodecimseritrevolutioi)". The scan clearly shows "56. 23." and "Duodecimae erit revolutio [Moon]" (apparently a misprint for Duodecima). The quoted "publice" is hyphenated pub-lice across lines, and 300 is printed in old-style figures.

Morin's latitude for Villefranche ("Polus 45. 25.") is 34' south of the modern 45d59'. This does not affect geocentric longitudes, only house cusps. The source gives no longitudes, so modern ones were used (+-0.05 deg = +-12 s of time).

Apparent to mean time used modern equation-of-time values for the epochs: -14.12 min on 1583-02-23 and -5.44 min on 1634-03-27. Horizons confirms them to 0.05 s. Morin's own Rudolphine equation of time and meridian corrections are not stated. The RAMC checks agree to about 5 s (1634) and about 27 s (1583, explained by the Rudolphine Sun error).
Dates are Gregorian (New Style), as Morin's Sun positions confirm. D.H.M. is astronomical reckoning from noon (22 Feb 20h33m = civil 23 Feb 08:33), as both RAMCs confirm.

Both instants lie outside the engine's reference span (1800-2200), and the results carry 'outside-reference-span'. Engine deltaT is 115.2 +- 24.5 s (1583) and 55.1 +- 18.9 s (1634), under 0.3' of Moon motion.
The birth time is Morin's own, probably rectified, time. The chain uses it exactly as stated.

Subject is deceased. The book's own 'Joannis Baptistae Morini Vita', p. XX (scan leaf 44), section CIV, says he died Monday 6 November 1656 at 2 a.m.: "die Lunae, sexto Novembris, hora post noctem mediam secunda, ejusdem anni 1656". English Wikipedia gives 6 Nov 1656, Paris. The work appeared posthumously in 1661.

verified.author: Jean-Baptiste Morin (1583-1656)
verified.title: Astrologia Gallica, Liber XXIII, Caput X (Morin's own lunar revolutions)
verified.page: p. 642 (intro, right column bottom) and p. 643 (figure, top). Scan leaves 724-725.
verified.subject: Jean-Baptiste Morin, the author
verified.explanation:
The 23.3 h gap comes from the printed figure, not from the engine.

**The book's own convention.** Pages 397 and 407 fix it: the day counts from noon and T.A. is apparent time ('tempore apparente'), with RAMC = apparent time + RA of the Sun. Read that way, the engine reproduces the printed RAMCs of the radix and of the 1634 and 1645 revolutions on the same pages to within 0.01-0.13°.

**The literal reading fails.** On that convention, '2. 23. 45' means 3 Nov 1642 at 11:45 LAT in Paris. The engine puts the Moon at 0°24'49" Aries then, 13.6° past the radical place. The figure itself prints ☽17 ♓.

**Everything else points to 2 Nov.** The figure's RAMC 217°15' (MC ♏9°40') occurs at Paris on 2 Nov 1642 at 11:32:36 UT (11:58 LAT, 11:42 LMT). At that moment the engine gives:

| Body | Engine | Printed |
|---|---|---|
| Sun | 10°10' Sco | 10 |
| Mercury | 25°09' Sco | 25 |
| Venus | 24°32' Sag | 24 |
| Mars | 8°28' Tau | 8 |
| Jupiter | 8°12' Pis | 9 |
| Saturn | 18°34' Pis | 18 |
| Moon | 16°32' Pis | 17 |
| Ascendant | 7°07' Cap | ♑8 |

The text says the ascendant is the opposition of radical Mars, which is ♋8°10' in the radix, so ♑8 fits. On 3 Nov, at the same RAMC, the engine has the Sun at 11°10' Sco and the Moon at 0°30' Aries. The text agrees with 2 Nov: Morin fell ill 'die 2 Novembris', 3 hours after the revolution.

**What is wrong in the print.** The printed day is one too many under the book's own convention, either a misprint or a slip into civil dating. The printed minutes also do not fit the printed RAMC: 11:45 against 11:58 LAT. 11:45 is close to the 11:42 LMT, as if the clock were mean time despite 'T.A.'.

**Engine figures.**
- Natal Moon at the stated birth: 16°48'36" Pis. Morin's Rudolphine radix gives 17°0', so the engine is 11.4' lower.
- Natal Sun: 4°11'52" against Morin's 4°19'18", 7.4' lower.
- Return to the engine's natal Moon: 2 Nov 12:00:50 UT (12:26 LAT Paris).
- Return to Morin's 17°0' Pis: 2 Nov 12:20:18 UT (12:46 LAT), which confirms the candidate's note.

**Even with the day corrected (not allowed),** the residual would be +25 to +41 min depending on the clock basis. Morin's 1634 and 1645 revolutions, read the same way from pp. 642-643, give +7.3 and −4.3 min.

**Subject.** Morin is the native and is dead. The Vita prefixed to this same 1661 edition (front matter p. XX, leaf 44) records his death on Monday 6 Nov 1656 ('sexto Novembris ... 1656'), about 2 a.m. His epitaph at Saint-Étienne-du-Mont is on p. XXI (leaf 45).

**Evidence.** Scans and crops are in <local> (f0725_center.jpg, f0725_figure.jpg, f0725_left.jpg, f0725_top.jpg, f0724_intro.jpg, f0479_natal_*.jpg, p0489_full1240.jpg, f0044_death.jpg).
issues: The printed instant contradicts its own figure. Read literally, '2. 23. 45' T.A. is 3 Nov 1642 11:45 LAT in Paris, when the Moon is at 0°25' Aries, not the printed 17 Pisces. The figure's planets, its RAMC 217°15' and the text ('die 2 Novembris', 3 hours later) all point to 2 Nov near noon.

The printed clock (23h45m) does not fit the printed RAMC 217°15', which implies about 23h58m apparent time on 2 Nov. The clock's time basis is therefore doubtful: apparent against mean differs by about 16 min of equation of time.

Using this example would mean correcting the printed day, and also the minutes or their time basis. The rules forbid fixing numbers, and no tolerance justified by the source covers the literal reading (23.3 h off).

Precision is low: the return Moon is printed to the degree only ('☽ 17'), and the radix Moon is 17°0' from the Rudolphine Tables (the radix figure says 'Ex Tabul. Rudolph.'; the return figure names no tables). Rudolphine minus engine at birth: Moon +11.4', Sun +7.4'.

The radix figure prints no sign glyph beside '☽17.0''. Its house placement (12th, ♓3°18' to ♈27°17') allows Pisces or Aries. Pisces follows from the return figures, which print ☽17 ♓, and from the engine's 16°48' Pis.
The source gives no longitude for the birthplace (only 'Polus 45. 25.', against a modern 45°59'). The modern 4.7186°E was used. Morin's own reduction on p. 407 is about 3 min earlier in UT.
Quote: the print reads 'difficelemque' (a misprint), not 'difficilemque' as transcribed in the candidate. All numbers match, as do the pages (642, 643, radix 397) and scan leaves (724, 725, 479).
Both instants are outside the engine's reference span (1800-2200) and carry the outside-reference-span flag. ΔT is 115 ± 24 s for 1583 and 49 ± 18 s for 1642, negligible here.

Leads, not verified here: Morin's 12th and 14th lunar revolutions on the same pages are internally consistent. They are p. 642 'Martii 27. 3. 20. T.A.' with RAMC 56.23, and p. 643 'Martii 25. 21. 42. T.A.' with RAMC 331.11. The engine gives RAMC 56.37 and 331.06, and the Sun at 6°56' against the printed 6.56. The engine's returns fall +7.3 min and −4.3 min from the printed instants, so these may merit a separate adversarial check.

verified.author: Jean-Baptiste Morin (1583-1656)
verified.title: Astrologia Gallica, Liber XXIII, Caput X (Morin's own lunar revolutions)
verified.page: p. 643: intro across both columns of the lower half; figure lower half. Scan leaf 725.
verified.subject: Jean-Baptiste Morin, the author
verified.explanation:
The engine's return is 256 s (4.3 min) earlier than Morin's. The difference comes from the source, not the engine. A JPL Horizons chain gives a natal Moon of 346.80347° at the same natal UT, and the Horizons Moon is 346.80314° at 09:34:04 UT, so a Horizons-based return falls within about 2 s of the engine's.

Morin worked from the Rudolphine Tables: the radix on p. 397 says 'Ex Tabul. Rudolph.', and cap. IX (p. 634) says the revolution is to be found in the same tables as the radical Moon, ignoring latitude. The mean time found there is then corrected for the equation of time and the meridian difference, giving the T.A. printed on the figure.
- His radical Moon, 17°0' Pisces, is 11.4' ahead of the engine's 16°48.6'.
- At his stated instant the engine Moon is at 16°51.2', so his tabular Moon was 8.84' ahead there.
- These two table errors nearly cancel. The residual is 2.55', and at the Moon's 35.9'/h that is 4.3 min, the whole difference.

Smaller effects:
- His Sun is 7.4' (1583) and 8.8' (1645) ahead of the modern Sun. That only shifts the RAMC-based conversions by about 30 s; with both instants converted that way the difference is -260 s.
- The minute rounding is worth ±30 s.

The near agreement is therefore largely fortuitous, not something the source's precision guarantees.
issues: Page check: p. 643 is scan leaf 725. The printed '643' has a smudged last digit, but leaves 724 and 726 read 642 and 644. The quote matches the print once long s and ligatures are normalised (the print splits 'prę-mium' across the line). The figure reads 1645 Martii D.H.M. 25.21.42 T.A. Parisiis: Moon 17 in the 10th house with Venus 8 and Mercury 8 Pisces, Sun 6.12, RAMC 331.11, Asc Cancer 1, MC Aquarius 29, Part of Fortune 11.48 Gemini. The engine's planets at the stated time agree with the figure to the degree.

Radix: p. 397 (leaf 479, Liber XVII) reads 1583 Februarii D.H.M. 22.20.33 T.A., Francopoli Bellerocensium, Polus 45.25, 'Ex Tabul. Rudolph.', RAMC 284.27, Moon 17.0'. No sign is printed next to the Moon; Pisces follows from the preceding new moon at Pisces 3°22' on 22 Feb, shown on the same page. The candidate left out the Rudolphine-tables note, which is what limits the tolerance.

Subject is deceased: the Vita in the same 1661 edition (p. XX, leaf 44) says Morin died on Monday 6 November 1656 at about 2 a.m., and p. XXI gives his epitaph. Wikipedia also gives 6 Nov 1656, Paris.

Chapter: Caput X ('vis Revolutionum Lunae ... in pluribus genituris', p. 634) covers several people's lunar revolutions, so it is not only Morin's own. This 14th one is his own ('datum mihi', 'inventione mea'), and p. 644 refers to 8 revolutions of his Moon. The next heading, on p. 644, is misprinted 'Caput II.' for XI.

The source gives no longitudes. Modern ones were used, and an error of ±0.02° would move the UT by about ±5 s. The printed natal latitude is about 34' south of Villefranche, but that does not affect the geocentric Moon.
The stated time is apparent time computed from tables, not observed. Converting it with the true equation of time and converting via Morin's printed RAMCs differ by 26-30 s, giving -256 s or -260 s.
Morin's printed radical Moon (347°00') is not the engine's (346°48.6'). Fed 347°00', lunarReturnInstant gives 09:53:07 UT, which is +887 s. A fixture has to use the whole chain.

The source says its lunar tables are inaccurate. Cap. IX (p. 634) says astronomers' Moons differ by almost 1°, about 2 h of lunar motion. P. 644 says accurate lunar tables did not yet exist. So no tolerance of a few minutes can be justified from the source. Sibling scratch results in this run for Morin's 1605 and 1612 revolutions show about -19 to -21 min; I did not re-verify them, but they fit this.
Engine flags 'outside-reference-span'. ΔT is 115 s ±24 for 1583 and 47 s ±18 for 1645.
Scratch files are in <local> morin-lr1645.mjs, morin-lr1645.out.json, horizons/moon.txt, and the page crops.

verified.author: Jean-Baptiste Morin (1583-1656)
verified.title: Astrologia Gallica, Liber XXIII, Caput X (examples of lunar revolutions)
verified.page: p. 644: intro top of right column; figure top; death date lower left column. Scan leaf 726.
verified.subject: Charles de Condren, Superior General of the Oratory ('B. Patris Caroli de Condren')
verified.explanation:
The difference is +5 h 07 min (engine minus stated). The cause is an error inside Morin's figure, not the engine.

Houses versus luminaries. The printed time and the houses agree with each other. RAMC '180. 38' and whole-degree cusps: Asc Sag 7, MC Lib 1, 11th Lib 27, 12th Sco 16, 2nd Cap 6, 3rd Aqu 20. At the stated instant the engine gives RAMC 181°32', Asc Sag 6°39', MC Lib 1°41', 11th Lib 27°23', 12th Sco 16°34', 2nd Cap 5°41', 3rd Aqu 20°30'.

The figure's own Sun (Sag 20°8') and Moon (Sco 28°10') belong to about five hours later. At the printed instant the engine has the Sun at Sag 19°55.4' and the Moon at Sco 25°05.1'. The engine Sun reaches 20°8' at 11:32:24 UT. The engine Moon reaches Morin's 28°10' at 11:29:43 UT, when the engine Sun is at 20°7.9'. So Morin's luminaries are consistent with about 11:30 UT, and his return moment from the tables agrees with the engine's return to about 12 min.

Why 12 min. Morin's Rudolphine radical Moon (Sco 28°10') is 7.65' below the engine's Moon for the stated birth instant. At the Moon's 37.6' per hour, 7.65' is about 12 min.

The natal chart is reproduced closely, so the tables were not the problem:
- Sun: Morin Sag 24°37', engine 24°37.4'.
- Moon: Morin Sco 28°10', engine 28°17.65'.
- Moon latitude: Morin '5. 1. S.' (S = septentrionalis, north), engine +5°0.8'.
- Cusps: 11th, 12th, 2nd and 3rd within about 5'.

Cause of the 5 h. Most likely a slip of about 5 h when Morin converted the tables' time to Paris apparent time and cast the houses (true value about 23h45m to 23h57m astronomical, printed 18h50m). It cannot be proven from the page, and the numbers must not be 'fixed'.

Morin's own reading depends on the erroneous houses: he puts the Sun in the 1st and the Moon in the 12th 'as in the radix'. At the true return the Sun is on the MC.

Precision the source claims for itself. Caput IX, p. 634, says the celebrated astronomers' lunar tables differed by 'fere unius gradus' (almost one degree), 'fere motus duarum horarum' (almost two hours of the Moon's motion). The end of Caput X, p. 644, also wishes for accurate lunar tables.
issues: The stated instant is 18425 s (5.1 h) before the engine's return. It is also 17694 s before the engine Moon reaches Morin's own radical value of Sco 28°10'.
The figure is internally inconsistent. The printed time and cusps fit about 06:35 UT, but the printed Sun (Sag 20°8') and Moon (Sco 28°10') fit about 11:30 UT.

RAMC '180. 38' corresponds to 18h46.4m apparent time, not the printed 18h50m (engine RAMC at 18h50m apparent: 181°32'). Cusps and most planets are whole degrees only; Morin, Caput V, p. 602, says he gives only whole degrees in revolutions.
Caput IX, p. 634: Morin says lunar tables differed by almost 1° (about 2 h of return time). Even that self-declared tolerance is exceeded, and it is too loose to test a lunar return.
The return figure prints no latitude. The nativity prints only 'Latit. 49' with no place. I took Vauxbuin's longitude from biographies; using Paris instead shifts the engine return by about 4 min.

'T.A.' is not spelled out on the page. I read it as apparent time from Morin's procedure in Caput V, p. 602 (mean time 'vertetur in apparens seu verum') and from the natal RAMC check. The choice is immaterial here (equation of time 5.8 min against a 5 h gap).

Correction to the candidate: the natal data are on p. 628 (leaf 710). The figure there prints the radical Moon as '28.10', Scorpio by house position between the 12th cusp Sco 18°18' and the Ascendant Sag 8°25'. It also prints Sun 24°37', RAMC 184°0', 'Ex Tab. Rudolph.'
Correction to the citation: the chapter heading after the example on p. 644 is misprinted 'CAPUT II.' (it should read XI). The examples are in Caput X, which starts on p. 634, leaf 716.

Death dates differ, but all say January 1641: Morin p. 644 gives 6 Jan 1641 about 6 a.m., the New Catholic Encyclopedia (M. J. Barry) gives Paris, 7 Jan 1641, and Wikipedia gives 17 Jan 1641. Deceased either way.
Natal Mars in the figure reads '♂ 4.58' (Libra, 10th house) against the engine's Libra 9°57'. That is probably a further figure or print error, though the 4/9 reading is not certain.
The engine flags outside-reference-span for 1588 and 1640. Its ΔT for 1588 is 105.6 s with σ 23.8 s, which does not matter at this scale.

verified.author: Unidentified hand in Richard Napier's casebooks (Bodleian MS Ashmole 204). Edited by Lauren Kassell, Michael Hawkins, Robert Ralley, John Young, Joanne Edge, Janet Yvonne Martin-Portugues and Natalie Kaoukji.
verified.title: The casebooks of Simon Forman and Richard Napier, 1596-1634: a digital edition. CASE79935 (Revolutions entry) with CASE79934 (Nativity).
verified.page: MS Ashmole 204, f. 47r: nativity at top of the folio (CASE79934), revolution in the middle (CASE79935)
verified.subject: Mr Richard Napier 'the nephew', i.e. Sir Richard Napier (PERSON18784)
verified.explanation:
The difference comes from the scribe's solar tables, not from the time basis. The edition does not transcribe the charts on f. 47r, but the IIIF images show the Sun at 15°9' Taurus in both the nativity and the revolution chart. The engine puts the Sun at 15°07.2' Taurus at 06:00 LMT London on 6 May 1607 (Gregorian), so the scribe is 1.8' ahead. At the stated 18:27 LMT on 5 May 1630 the engine has 15°04.4', so the scribe is 4.6' ahead. That error grew by 2.86' between the two dates (the engine's Sun at the stated instant is 171.4" short of its own natal Sun). At the Sun's speed of 2.414'/h, 2.86' is exactly the 71.0 min.

The time basis barely matters. Using apparent time at both ends shifts both ends by about 3.8 min (equation of time +3.83 and +3.80 min), leaving 4258 s. Casting the revolution at Great Linford instead of London gives 4099 s.

The stated clock time is itself consistent. The revolution chart's Ascendant, 4°20' Scorpio, is reached at London at 18:21:30 LMT by the engine, 5.5 min before the stated time (about 2 min if the time is apparent time).

The entry does not name its tables, and other bodies in the same charts are off by up to about 2.4°. In the revolution chart, Venus is 14°2' Taurus against the engine's 11°40.7', and Mercury is 22°51' Aries against 20°39.2'. Giving the engine the source's own 15°9' yields 20:22:50 UT, 115 min after the stated time, so the 1630 table error carries most of the gap.

The nativity is given only to the hour. A ±30 min uncertainty in birth time moves the engine's return by the same ±30 min (+41 to +101 min against the stated time). A later revolution for the same native (CASE76838, 1633, 'h. 3. p. m.', hour only) comes out 118 min later than the engine's return from the same nativity, which is the opposite sign. So the revolutions recorded for this native scatter by hours around the modern value.
issues: Verdict: engine minus stated is +4259 s (+71.0 min) with LMT at London at both ends. It is +4258 s if both times are apparent time, and +4099 s if the revolution was cast for Great Linford. This exceeds the roughly 1 h bar for a solar return.

Confirmed against the edition and the manuscript image: CASE79935 reads 'Revolutio Anni Etatis 24 inchoantis 25 Aprilis i630. Horæ 6 Min. 27 P. M.', and CASE79934 reads 'Mr Richard Napier Aprilis 26. ☉ hor. 6. a. mē i607.' Both are on MS Ashmole 204, f. 47r (nativity at the top, revolution in the middle). The IIIF image MS-ASHMOLE-00204-000-00117 shows the same numerals clearly; the edition's 'i607' and 'i630' render the scribe's j-shaped 1. Minor point: the manuscript spells the surname 'Naper', where the edition prints 'Napier'.
Calendar checks: 26 Apr 1607 (Julian) was a Sunday, matching '☉'. 28 Aug 1630 (Julian) was a Saturday, matching the horary's '♄' on the same folio. 25 Apr 1630 (Julian) was a Sunday.
Folio 47r states no place, meridian or time basis for the revolution. London at 51°30'N is inferred from the related nativities CASE52110, CASE67595 and CASE79994; the longitude 0°06'W is assumed.

The nativity is stated only to the hour ('hor. 6. a. mē'). The person page also lists 1607-04-25 06:00, 1607-04-26 06:06 and 1607-01-23 23:59. The 06:06 time is Gravius's in CASE25864 ('h. 6 6′ Mat.', 'equated' to 5h55m and 'reduced to the Frankfurt meridian' as 7h2m). Entries reading 'Apr 25 ... hor. 18 p m' count hours from noon, which is 26 Apr 06:00 civil time, so the edition's '1607-04-25 (06:00)' looks like a conversion slip.

The radical and revolution Sun longitudes are not in the edition's transcription; I read 15°9' Taurus in both from the chart images. The engine's natal Sun is 45.1202° (15°07.2' Taurus), 1.8' below the source. The engine's Sun at the stated instant is 15°04.4' Taurus, 4.6' below.

The source names no tables, and other bodies in the same charts are off by up to about 2.4°: revolution Venus +2°21' and Mercury +2°12'; natal Saturn 19°34' Capricorn against the engine's 18°44.4'. The source therefore cannot bound the tables' solar error, which here drifted about 2.9' between 1607 and 1630.

Death is not recorded in the casebooks edition (person page: 'Not recorded in the casebooks'). It comes from the Dictionary of National Biography vol. 40 (1894), Sidney Lee's article 'Napier, Richard', which also covers Sir Richard Napier (1607-1676). Read on Wikisource at Page:Dictionary_of_National_Biography_volume_40.djvu/78; the printed page number is not confirmed. It says he was 'born in London in 1607' and 'died ... on 17 Jan. 1675-6, and was buried in Great Linford Church'. Being born in 1607, he is necessarily dead in any case.
The engine flags both instants outside-reference-span (before 1800). ΔT at 1607 is 80.2 s ± 21.8 s (reconstructed segment); its effect on this comparison is under a minute.

Cross-check: the 1633 revolution for the same native (CASE76838, MS Ashmole 214 p. 422, hour only) is 118 min later than the engine's 1633 return from the same nativity. That is the opposite sign to the 1630 entry.
Scratch files: <local> and napier1630-sr.out.json in the same folder. Manuscript crops are in <local> No repository file was modified.

verified.author: Richard Napier (1559-1634), astrologer-physician. Edited by Lauren Kassell, Michael Hawkins, Robert Ralley, John Young, Joanne Edge, Janet Yvonne Martin-Portugues and Natalie Kaoukji.
verified.title: The casebooks of Simon Forman and Richard Napier, 1596-1634: a digital edition. CASE32724 (Revolutions entry) with CASE32723 (Nativity).
verified.page: MS Ashmole 229, f. 19r: nativity upper left (CASE32723), revolution top right (CASE32724)
verified.subject: Lady Constable [Dormer] (PERSON22643)
verified.explanation: The engine's return is 4 h 39 min (16,762 s) earlier than Napier's. The cause is Napier's solar positions, not the time basis, the calendar or the place. On the manuscript page, Napier puts the Sun at 1 deg 34' Virgo both in the nativity and in both revolution figures; the edition transcribes the figures only as chart placeholders, so I read these from the page image. The engine puts the Sun at 1 deg 37.67' Virgo at his stated birth instant, so Napier's natal Sun is 3.67' lower. At his stated return instant the engine has the Sun at 1 deg 48.93' Virgo, so his 1607 Sun is 14.93' lower. The 11.26' difference between those two offsets is 4.66 h of solar motion at 0.9676 deg/day, which is the whole gap. In other words, the source Napier used for 1607 placed the Sun about 15' behind the engine, and his 1562 source about 4' behind. He then took the hour when his 1607 Sun reached 1 deg 34' Virgo; his sum 10.14 + 4 = 14.14 confirms 4 p.m. apparent time. The source does not name his tables or ephemerides. Asked when the Sun reaches Napier's own 1 deg 34' Virgo in 1607, the engine answers 09:54 UTC, 6.17 h before his 4 p.m. By comparison, the Old Style dates (both Saturdays, as Napier marks), apparent versus mean time (equation of time -1.6 min) and the unstated English place (minutes) are negligible.

selection.coverage: Solar returns: covered by 8 fixtures. Seven are whole-chain (stated birth instant, then the engine's natal Sun, then the engine's return). Five of these are post-1800, with source-derived tolerances of 30-100 s: Leo 1910 and 1907, Green 1893, Raphael 1906, Astrolabus 1908. Two are pre-1800, at 800 s and 2217 s: Gadbury 1648 and Lilly 1646. The eighth is return-step only: Green 1900, solarReturnInstant from a stated radical, 60 s. Lunar returns: covered only at the return-step level, by one fixture: Green 1904, lunarReturnInstant from the stated radical Moon 3°34′ Gemini, 2 Jan 1901, 130 s. No verified lunar candidate states a birth instant, so the full lunarReturn(birth, ...) chain has no worked-example fixture. Planetary returns: not covered. No planetary-return worked example was among the verified candidates, so there is no fixture and the gap remains open.

Not included, and the tolerance was not widened: Pearce, The Science of the Stars (1881), p. 124 (Queen Victoria, 1854 return). The verifier's 900 s rests on JPL Horizons measurements of Pearce's tables (his 1819 noon Suns are 13-14″ low), not on the source. A budget from the source alone is about ±142 s: radical printed to 1″ (12.5 s), the 1819 noon places to 1″ (12.5 s), his own proportion slip of 39′4″ for 39′2.03″ (49 s), his own birth-meridian inconsistency (51 s), the unprinted 1854 working at the same precision (about 16 s), and the printed second. The engine is +261.2 s with the birth read as LMT at 51s W, or +210.2 s read as GMT (both re-run here), so it is outside that budget on either reading. The engine matches Horizons to 0.12″ at the birth, so the gap lies in Pearce's tables, but the source alone cannot show that.

Not included, and the tolerance was not widened: Coley, Clavis Astrologiae Elimata (2nd ed., 1676), pp. 703-705 (1678 return). The verifier's 1800 s is built from modern physics, not from the source: nutation (unknown before 1748), the Earth-Moon and planetary terms, and the Caroline table year being 12.4 s per year longer than the modern tropical year. The source gives the instant to the second by adding table intervals, and it does not size its own simplification (anomaly 265°20′ entered as 270°, without the equation). No tolerance the source alone justifies covers the engine's -771.7 s. The verifier's itemised breakdown reproduces the gap to within 44 s, so the gap reflects the 1661 tables rather than the engine.

Reported, not widened: Green's Map No. 3 lunar return (18 Nov 1899, 1.49 a.m., Modern Astrology New Series Vol. I p. 278) has the same author and radical Moon as the chosen 1901 fixture. It was not a verified candidate, but the verifier of its sibling reports engine minus stated = -143 s (about -188 s on the mean-time reading). That is outside the 130 s budget the series' stated precision supports. The 130 s on the chosen lunar fixture is therefore the source's stated precision, not a guarantee of the author's interpolation.

There is no whole-chain fixture for Green 1903, because the book states no birth instant. Combining its return with the London Gazette's birth time gives +66.2 s (10:48 read as LMT) or +32.2 s (read as GMT), and the first is outside the 60 s step tolerance. Because that birth time does not come from the source, the combination was not adopted and the tolerance was not widened.

Duplicates and near-duplicates dropped. Green 1903 was supplied twice and is merged into one fixture. Zadkiel's Ada example is one example in two printings (Grammar of Astrology 1833, pp. 124-125; Bohn 1852, p. 441). It passes on both time-basis readings (-152.5 s as mean time, +277.6 s as apparent time, within its source-derived 600-740 s), but was dropped for low precision: the instant is not worked on the page, the author says only that it can be estimated closely, and the two readings differ by 429 s. Lilly's 1658, 1662, 1663, 1664 and 1665 returns for the same merchant were dropped in favour of the fully worked 1646 one; the 1662-1665 times are the 1658 time plus constant 365d 5h 49m steps. Their residuals (-954, -479, -223, -295 and +52 s) are inside their source-derived 1440-1800 s tolerances. Green's 15 Dec 1899 lunar return (same radical and series) was dropped because it is printed as 10 a.m. with no minutes and no map, so the source cannot rule out rounding to the hour; it passes at -42.2 s.

Dropped for precision or method, although they pass. Simmonite [1854] (Victoria 1854, +799.6 s within ±1800 s): the radical is given only to the arc-minute (evidently truncated), three conflicting return times are printed, and it is the same 1854 return as Pearce's. Gadbury, Genethlialogia (1658), p. 267 (-30.3 s within ±600 s): the instant is read from a perpetual table that the author says he uses for ease rather than exactness, and per its verifier an engine without nutation would also pass (about +597 s), so the fixture has little power. Occult Review, Nov 1917, p. 257 (George V 1918, +197 s within the proposed 360 s): the page states no nativity (the birth time comes from the Edinburgh Gazette), no year and no time basis, and George V is already covered by Green 1905.

Raphael's tolerance is set to 100 s instead of the verifier's 120 s. 100 s is the recomputed worst case of 96.1 s rounded up; the verifier's extra margin was not derived from the source, and the engine (+59.7 s) does not need it.

Input conventions. All instants are UT (UT1 before 1972; the engine reads pre-1972 utc input as UT1). Whole-chain fixtures must pass the natal instant, so that the engine derives its own natal longitude. For the two pre-1800 fixtures this is essential: their tables are 6-7′ off, and only that offset cancels. Feeding the source's radical instead puts the return hours off (Lilly's 6°37′: about 184 min early; Gadbury's 22°27′: about 152 min late). The two return-step fixtures (Green 1903, Green 1904) must pass the stated radical longitude, not a birth instant.

The two pre-1800 fixtures (Lilly 1646, Gadbury 1648) are kept only to cover that period; no more precise pre-1800 example was among the candidates. Both lie outside the engine's REFERENCE_SPAN (1800-2200): results carry outside-reference-span, ΔT comes from the reconstructed segment (about 59-70 s, σ about 20 s), and the site clips return searches to 1800-2200. They belong in the package-level suite and should expect the flag. Their tolerances (2217 s and 800 s) catch only gross errors (wrong calendar, hour or year, or a sidereal/tropical mix-up) and do not cover table drift that the sources cannot bound.

Several time bases are inferred rather than stated. Leo III: London clock time is entered as Greenwich time, as Leo does. Green 1903 and Green 1904: times labelled London are read as GMT, and the tolerances include the London or Kensington mean-time alternative. Raphael 1905: the birth is read as GMT under the author's p. 34 rule; the LMT reading gives +90.3 s, inside 100 s. Astrolabus 1908: the return is read as GMT; an Ipswich-mean-time reading (+279 s) is not covered. Lilly 1646: Frankfurt an der Oder is assumed for Origanus's meridian, and the difference does not depend on it. Gadbury 1648: apparent time and 0°06′ W are assumed, and the difference does not depend on the longitude.

Provenance gaps. The Leo examples were verified only in the 1936 5th edition; their 1913 2nd-edition origin is unverified. The 1904 date and New Series Vol. I for the Green lunar article come from Google Books metadata, because the title page was not seen. Leo III uses Leo's rectified 5.29 p.m. birth time (her autobiography gives 5.39 p.m.). Every fixture uses the birth time as its own source states it.

The seven fixtures with tolerances of 130 s or less cluster together. All their returns fall in 1893-1910, at London-area latitudes of 51.5-52.1° N. Five come from the Modern Astrology circle of 1903-1913 (Leo, Green) and two from the London Foulsham press (Raphael 1905, Old Moore's 1908). They probably used Nautical-Almanac-derived ephemerides, so their table errors may be correlated.

The tolerances for the sources that print times only to the minute (Green 1905, Green 1904, Raphael, Astrolabus) assume the minute was rounded, not truncated. Truncation would widen the Astrolabus bound to about 85-90 s. Every observed difference passes under either assumption.
